# jj help routing decision record

The first version said only, "Don't maintain another table of help names." That still holds after review, but it did not settle the routing order. Getting names from the command structure does not mean flattening that structure into a list of names and then passing it through string filtering; the fragments the user has already entered change the scope to look at next.

## The original starting point still stands

`completers/jj_completer/cmd/help_move.go` can still serve as a reference point for a focused check. The visible file header contains only `package cmd` and a `import (` block, so the file is at least near command completion. The earlier claim that "this file handles help" was too strong. It is now retained in a weaker form: investigations involving help, move, changes, or revision can start here to enter the command package, then inspect the actual references.

The original reason for rejecting a separate name table has not changed either. If the completion layer keeps its own command names, short names, and descriptions, any change to a command's position leaves two places where names and hierarchy must be synchronized. This is less apparent with single-level input; once namespaces appear, the completion side also has to interpret which words allow further input and which are just endpoints.

Another option, not listed separately at the time, was a flat list: get all names from the command side, but do not retain their positions in the candidates, and let the caller process them by spaces or prefixes. This removes one layer of maintenance compared with a handwritten list, but still erases path relationships. Ordinary commands under the root may appear to work, while nested input leaves later rules to guess "which parent command are we after now?"

## Distinctions added during review

The review split the discussion into two adjacent concerns.

The first is recognition. Words already entered may refer to an ordinary command, a namespace that still has subcommands, or merely an old name. Presentation comes second: which next-segment names to offer after the identified position, and how to display the candidates. Reversing that order—generating candidates first and then inferring hierarchy from their text—removes the basis for making that distinction when names are identical or have similar prefixes.

A review note at the time read:

> First identify the node where the input stops; candidates are the next step after that node, not names pulled from a global word list with parents filled in afterward.

This does not require entering a subtree for every word that has already matched. Leaf commands and namespaces that can be expanded further play different roles. The former can end the path; only the latter provide the local scope for the next segment. The old notes called both kinds of object "command names," obscuring the distinction.

Aliases should not automatically become a third source of candidates either. If an alias represents a reachable path in the command tree, it can participate in selection at that position; if it is merely a name left in help text, treating it as an entry point that can be expanded further creates a false expectation. The earlier statement that "all aliases should be completable" no longer applies, because it did not first establish the relationship between an alias and its command position.

## Retained earlier proposal

The passage below comes from the earlier approach. It is retained to explain why simple input seemed sufficient at the time; it is no longer the adopted approach.

> Collect common help names and aliases; split the input on spaces; filter names using the remaining text; when a name contains spaces, expand it within the same set.

This can account for a single input segment under the root. The problem is in the last clause: hierarchy is reconstructed only after candidate generation, and the shared set no longer knows which parent position the user has passed through. Name length is not the issue; the input path has already changed the candidate scope.

Another idea that was not adopted was to display only leaf commands. This would avoid the debate over whether namespaces can be displayed and would shorten the candidate list; the cost is that namespaces themselves lose their entry points, and users under help cannot see positions where they can continue typing. This approach was not retained as a compatibility layer.

## Discussion of `amend`

In the earlier discussion, `amend` was treated as an example of how "candidate descriptions can be hardcoded on the completion side." It only shows that candidates need descriptions; it does not establish that descriptions should be copied into a separate table. If descriptions are detached from the selected command position, command moves, alias display, and nested paths will each drift independently.

This round therefore keeps the command structure as the primary source and adds an order of operations: first locate the command position based on the help path already entered; take candidates from its child scope only if that position can actually be expanded further; use the root scope only while still at the entry position. Aliases do not get an independent pool; they are handled according to whether they represent a reachable position in the path being entered.

The specific call sites in the visible file, and whether all existing aliases have the same path properties, remain unconfirmed. The filename `help_move.go` alone cannot substitute for either check.

# jj help Routing Decision Record

This record did not start with a complete set of rules. It began as a narrow decision about help candidates, then accumulated review notes, a revised position after a follow-up review, two now-outdated examples, and questions that have yet to be split out. Older sections retain their original time context; they explain the tradeoffs made then and should not be read as descriptions of the implementation today.

The local path available for reference remains `completers/jj_completer/cmd/help_move.go`. It has come up repeatedly in connection with help, move, changes, and revision. The visible portion of the file belongs to `package cmd`, followed by a `import (` block. That is enough to direct the investigation toward command completion, but not to infer from the filename that this is the central control point for help. For actual changes, references within the command package still need to be traced to determine where they belong.

The scope of this page has also remained narrow: paths, aliases, and nested namespaces after `jj help`. Configuration keys and environment variables are not decided here. The concern is not whether a command can execute, but whether the candidate list stays at the correct position in the command hierarchy as the user types one segment at a time.

## 2023-04-03: Initial Tradeoff

The initial record came from a straightforward concern: if the completion code maintained its own command names, aliases, and descriptions, it would gradually become a second registry alongside the command package. This duplication is not obvious when a root command has just been added. Once short names, old names, and multi-segment commands are mixed together, maintainers have to decide which side owns each name, description, and parent-child relationship.

Three approaches were listed at the time, but only the first-level decision was recorded.

**Separate name table.** Store names, aliases, and display descriptions individually on the completion side. This makes local edits quick and output formatting easy to standardize. The problem is not simply "a few extra lines": once a name moves into a namespace, the table also has to restate the parent-child relationship; when the same word appears under different paths, the table has no inherent place to anchor it.

**Flat set of names.** Rather than hand-maintaining every name, flatten the names obtained from the command side into a set, then filter by prefix against the text already entered. This appears to avoid manual maintenance, but still reduces paths to text. Asking "where did this originally belong?" only after generating candidates requires another set of rules to reconstruct the hierarchy.

**Local candidates from the current position.** First determine where the user has reached in the command tree, then list the next segment from there. This was not written up as a complete implementation plan, because the specific behavior of aliases, leaf commands, and namespaces had not yet been confirmed. It did, however, preserve the parent-child relationships already defined by the commands themselves.

That decision amounted to just one sentence: do not use a separately maintained, long-lived help name table. It ruled out the first approach; it did not automatically settle all the details of the other two. In particular, "names stay with commands" must not be read as "every name in the tree is displayed directly," nor does it imply that an alias necessarily allows further input in the same way as the command's primary name.

`move` is the only recurring counterexample in the first draft. Taken as a name on its own, it is easy to match by prefix; put back into the help input context, we still need to distinguish whether the user is at the root, has already entered a namespace, or has reached a command that cannot be expanded further. The first draft did not resolve this. It only pointed out that flattening names before filtering puts the parent-child relationship in the wrong order.

The first draft left four questions unanswered: whether aliases follow the command's position; whether candidates for nested input should come from the parent position or the global set; where the description for `amend` should come from; and where `help_move.go` sits in an actual invocation. Looking back, these questions fall into three categories—routing, display, and references—and should not be lumped into one broad issue of "help completion isn't done properly."

## 2023-04-04: Notes in the review margins

The review did not ask for candidates to be put into a fixed format immediately. It pointed out that the first draft had mixed recognition and presentation in a single paragraph.

The recognition question is: what does the text entered so far point to? It may resolve to an ordinary command, a namespace with subcommands, or only an old name left in the help text. The presentation question is: once the position is established, which names can be listed for the next segment, and how should candidate descriptions follow them? If presentation comes first and recognition is added afterward, the result is often a plausible-looking set of names with no indication of whether they belong to the root, a parent command, or an invalid old path.

The review's exact wording was:

> First determine which command node the input has stopped at. Candidates are not pulled from a word list; they belong to the next step after a particular node.

At the time, this margin note was only correcting the reading order. It was later misread as "enter the subtree whenever any word matches." These are different. A leaf command can be the endpoint of the path being entered; only a node with subcommands can potentially provide a local scope for subsequent input. Treating both kinds of objects as ordinary candidates makes the implementation display an endpoint while pretending it can still be expanded.

Another margin note concerned aliases. The first draft assumed aliases would appear alongside canonical names in the candidate list, which naturally made them look like the same kind of entry point. The review found insufficient grounds for that assumption: if an alias really represents a reachable path in the tree, it can appear at that position; if it is merely a historical name in the help text, text similarity alone should not make it a routing entry point from which input can continue. This did not decide how all aliases should be displayed. It only decided not to treat "aliases" as a third tree detached from command positions.

The same review round also narrowed the role of `help_move.go`. It is a local entry point for finding the term at issue, not a file that establishes all help branch relationships. This limitation does not diminish the path's value; it prevents readers from treating move as the source of rules for other commands just because the filename contains move.

## 2023-11-27: How a single-level example misled

The subsequent review did not produce a candidate table that could cover every command. Instead, it exposed why the old approach had looked credible on simple input. That approach split the input on spaces and looked for matches in a set of names. With just one segment entered at the root, it produced readable results, and the candidates looked as though they came from the command structure. The observations at the time were not baseless.

The problems started with namespaces. A flat set could still return items with the same prefix, so what was missing was not necessarily visible at a glance. But the set did not know which parent node the user had already passed through. If a later step then used spaces or separators in the names to "expand one level," the hierarchy was being added back only after the candidates had been generated. The same segment could mean different things at the root and in a nested position, but the flat set did not preserve that distinction.

Early notes summarized this as "long names need one more expansion." That explanation was later rejected. The difficulty was not how many segments a name had, but how the input path changed the scope from which candidates should come. A short name could also sit under a namespace; a multi-segment display name did not necessarily mean the input had successfully located a position. Using length, the number of spaces, or the prefix itself in place of determining position would all reduce routing to string manipulation.

The following procedure was retained at the time:

> Collect common help names and aliases; split the input on spaces; filter names using the remaining text; when a name contains spaces, continue expanding within the same set.

This passage is now marked as deprecated, but has not been deleted. It records why the initial demo passed: a single segment at the root did not force the set to answer where the parent node was. The last clause in particular no longer applies. The same set is not a reliable "next level," because the candidates had already lost the user's position when they entered the set.

There was also a proposal to "show only leaf commands." It would shorten the candidate list and sidestep the debate over whether namespaces could be displayed. The proposal was not adopted. A namespace is not superfluous intermediate text: users enter it after help precisely to get the local choices available beyond that position. Keeping only leaves would remove those entry points and make a state in which users could continue typing look as though there were no next step.

## 2023-11-27: Another debate over descriptions

`amend` came into the discussion because it had a specific description. Early on, someone used this to argue that candidate descriptions should be stored directly on the completion side. That would make output stable and avoid having to consult the command object each time. The argument addressed a real need—candidates should not just be a list of bare names—but turned "we need descriptions" into "we need copies of descriptions."

Copying descriptions would separate the display text from the command's position. If a command moved, an alias changed how it was displayed, or the same name was selected under different paths, the copy on the completion side would no longer inherently know which position it belonged to. The sentence "Descriptions can be stored in the candidate table" was later struck from the old draft, not because descriptions were unimportant, but because a description should follow the selected command position rather than first becoming content in another catalog.

An exchange that was never incorporated into the formal review is retained below:

> Q: Should an alias and its canonical name have two separate descriptions?
>
> A: First confirm whether they point to the same command position. Until the position is established, discussing two descriptions is pointless.

This Q&A does not claim that aliases can never have different displays. It only puts the decision order back in the right sequence: establish routing and reachability first, then decide how candidates should be presented. The old draft did the opposite, comparing display forms first and inferring the path from them.

`move` was also repositioned at this stage. It appears on this page not because move can represent all help behavior, but because the initial path lookup included this name. It helps expose a distinction: identical candidate text does not mean that the candidate is reachable on the current path. The former can result from filtering; the latter requires a command position. That distinction is more worth preserving than adding a special rule for move.

## Retained but no longer adopted approaches

The two approaches in the old record have not been removed, because each can seem reasonable in a local context.

The first is "root set first": always list all visible names under the root, then exclude entries that do not match the input text. This is suitable when the input is still at the root position, so root candidates cannot be said to be always wrong. The problem is that once the user has entered a namespace, it brings entries that do not belong to the current position back into the results. The root set is a scope, not a default source available at every stage.

The second is "alias first": show aliases that are easier for users to remember first, then add the parent position if necessary. This conflates memorability with command reachability as a single condition. An alias can be one display form of a candidate, but it cannot skip the step of determining the parent position. If aliases are made responsible for hierarchical jumps first, the completion side will start maintaining a shadow tree held together by string conventions.

Neither approach created a compatibility commitment. Retaining them does not require the implementation to continue supporting dedicated branches; it serves as a reminder for future changes: single-level display behavior, candidate count, and the convenience of user memory cannot individually prove that nested routing is correct.

## 2025-09-09: Revised wording after review

This review explicitly changed the early judgment—"list all candidates from the root, then filter"—to a conditional approach. The root scope applies only when the input has not yet been resolved to a command position that can be expanded further. Once it has been resolved to a namespace, falling back to the global name set loses the current path; conversely, assuming that a subtree exists before the input has been resolved hides the root entry too early.

So the first question should be a smaller, checkable one: has the current input already matched a parent position with subcommands? If it has not, we should not pretend that we have entered a subtree; if it has, the candidate scope should not revert to the root set. This revised wording carries forward the original decision not to maintain a second name table, while filling in the selection order that was not written down at the time.

The old wording about aliases is also corrected here. "Show it as long as the alias matches" only says that the text can match; it does not say that the alias is reachable on the current path. The current handling does not construct a route starting from the alias name. It first considers the alias's relationship to the command position. That avoids adding a separate parent-level jump for every alias, and avoids mistaking an old name for the next entry in the path merely because the old wording is still present.

The state diagram below retains only the shape of the decision; it is not a line-by-line description of `help_move.go`:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Root position: Namespace not yet located
    Root position --> Matching parent position: Input corresponds to a node that can be continued
    Root position --> Root-scope candidate: No matching parent position
    Matching parent position --> Local-scope candidate
    Root-scope candidate --> [*]
    Local-scope candidate --> [*]
```

"Matching parent position" in the diagram is not a state reached after an arbitrary prefix match. It requires the position corresponding to the input to actually have subcommands. The old flat approach has difficulty preserving this constraint naturally because it first produces a collection of text candidates and only afterward attempts to recover the hierarchy from the text.

## Issues Not Yet Split Out

After route selection has been tightened, one adjacent issue remains outside the scope of this page: for display names made up of multiple words and users entering them segment by segment, when should a continuation prompt be provided, and when should only terminal candidates be provided? It is related to namespaces but is not the same as selecting the root scope and parent scope; do not add another layer of manual jump rules just to fill this gap.

Another unresolved item is how the local file is actually connected. `help_move.go` provides an entry point for tracing back, but the file header itself cannot replace the call graph. Changes involving this file should be assessed based on references in the command package; do not centralize all help issues here merely because their names are similar.

These two issues do not change the decisions already made: do not maintain a second global name table, do not use post-hoc string splitting in place of nested-position checks, and do not make aliases solely responsible for parent-child relationships.

## Disagreement Left from Review

The following review excerpt has remained in place:

> "Content already present in the tree is not necessarily suitable for direct display."
>
> "Yes, but finding a position in the tree first and dumping the tree as-is are two different things."

The first sentence reminds us that the command structure and the candidate interface are not the same object; the second explains that the structure is still the source for selection, not a reason to display every node unconditionally. The two sentences were once interpreted as contradicting each other, so the discussion returned to an independent name table. It was only later clarified that they address different levels: one concerns where to select from, and the other concerns how to present the result after selection.

Another old objection was whether deriving candidates from the structure would make the completion layer take on too much routing logic. This concern remains, but the conclusion is not to return to a flat list. The completion layer needs to select the appropriate command position based on the path already entered; it does not need to recreate a tree maintained through string conventions. The boundary is not the amount of logic, but whether the relationship is already provided by the command structure.

## Current Decision

The earlier draft, margin annotations, and old examples cannot replace this requirement:

The jj help positional completer must derive candidates from the live Cobra command tree, select the matching parent tree for nested namespaces, and expose amend with description 'Move changes from a revision into its parent'.

The order of these requirements is not interchangeable. Candidates must come from the live Cobra command tree, not from a backlog of command copies on the completion side; for nested namespaces, first select the matching parent tree rather than adding a layer by name after filtering the global candidates; the description of `amend` must appear as the display text for that candidate and must not be replaced with the old generic wording.

Alias handling stays within the same boundary: whether an alias appears must be determined by its position in the current command tree and current path, rather than by first building an alias pool that is always available. If an old name no longer represents a reachable location, it must not be treated as an entry point that can still be used merely because the old help text remains.

The implementation changes only need to return to three checks: does the candidate come from the live tree; does the namespace already entered carry the scope to the corresponding parent tree; and does `amend` carry the required description. Early examples can explain why these checks are needed, but cannot replace them.

## Appendix: Archived Old Examples

**Old example 1: Global short-name priority.**

The old draft assumed that showing the shortest names first whenever the user entered an arbitrary prefix would reduce the candidate set. This example ignored where the short name was located. A short name being available under the root does not mean it remains available under an already entered namespace. "Shortest" is no longer used as a routing criterion.

**Old example 2: Alias before parent node.**

The old draft assumed that aliases were easier to remember and therefore suitable as path entry points. This example conflated ease of recall with command reachability. The current order is to determine the parent location first, then decide the candidate form; an alias is not a shortcut around the parent location.

Neither old example constitutes a compatibility requirement. They are retained to prevent the same intuition from becoming a proposal again under different wording: candidates that look reasonable for simple input do not mean that nested input is positioned correctly.

# JJ Environment Configuration Interface Proposal

This round starts with two entry points that are easy to conflate: environment variables are a set of names that can be determined before the process starts; dotted configuration keys need continued completion after the user has entered a configuration context. Treating both as ordinary filename candidates would mix paths, commands, and configuration hierarchies together.

The tentative plan is to put environment variables in a registry gated on the presence of the jj executable. This condition is not meant to inspect configuration file contents, but to avoid leaving apparently usable candidates on machines without jj. Value completion should not take the same form for every variable, either: configuration file locations should accept file paths, while editor locations should accept commands and their subsequent arguments.

For dotted configuration keys, we will not start by scanning local configuration files. Scanning can provide keys the user has already written, but it brings machine state into the candidates and misses keys available in the defaults that have not yet been written to disk. The initial draft proposes maintaining a finite set of key names and using the dot as the separator for entering the next level.

There are two options:

- Offer dotted keys only under configuration subcommands, reducing noise in ordinary argument positions;
- Share one set of key names across all entry points that accept configuration overrides, so callers no longer have to assemble strings individually.

The preference is currently for the first option. The second requires listing which entry points actually accept overrides first; otherwise, completion would suggest unsupported arguments with too much certainty.

The rollback conditions should also be explicit: if the environment variable registry needs to depend on configuration key scanning to work, split the two parts back into their own entry points; if dotted keys cannot continue to the next level in a real configuration workflow, stop maintaining the static set and recheck where the keys should come from.

Still to fill in: the suffix for editor candidates when a space is encountered; whether configuration keys include read-only items; whether the command tree should retain any environment variable hints when the jj executable is absent.

# JJ Environment Configuration Interface Proposal

The initial draft framed the problem as two candidate tables, "environment variables" and "configuration keys." After review, that looks too tidy. Values for the former take different input forms, and the difficulty with the latter is not the dot itself, but which positions give a key name meaning.

During review, `pkg/actions/fs/extension.go` was also noted. This location belongs to the `fs` package, and the file header provides only clues from adjacent imports. It is a useful place to continue tracing the connection between file and command completion, but it does not support classifying dotted configuration keys as part of file-extension logic. The original claim that "scanning configuration files is enough to provide completion" is therefore retained here as a direction we did not adopt, no longer as an implementation premise.

The recommendation is still to register environment variables separately, but v1's "show everything if jj is present" needs to be narrowed. Executable availability only gates the registry; candidates for each variable's value still need to be chosen according to what it actually accepts. Configuration locations accept filenames; editors accept commands. Sending editors through file completion as well would prevent existing commands from accepting further arguments; conversely, sending configuration locations through command completion would distort directory and filename selection.

Two candidate approaches remain for dotted keys:

1. Maintain a finite set of known key names, with the configuration entry point deciding whether to offer candidates;
2. Obtain key names from configuration sources visible at runtime, then collapse them into hierarchical candidates.

The first approach gives stable candidates without depending on the user's working directory. Its drawback is that new keys need to be synced manually. The second is closer to the actual settings, but configuration sources may vary with the working directory, user files, and defaults, so candidates will differ across machines. This revision neither combines the two approaches nor assumes either has already been made to work.

The review left one disagreement about actual usage unresolved: some people want complete keys suggested before the user reaches the first dot, to make settings easier to discover; the other view is to offer the top level first and let the dot bring up the next level, keeping candidates shorter. The former is helpful for uncommon keys; the latter is less likely to fill the list with long key names. The design follows the latter approach for the time being, until we can see how real configuration entry points accept the hierarchy.

The v1 boundary of "offer them only under configuration subcommands" is also insufficient. The real question is whether the argument position interprets the input as a configuration key, not whether the command name contains config. If an override argument accepts the same key format, it should be able to reuse the candidates; if an argument accepts only paths, it should not receive key names even when it is near a configuration command.

This revision does not extend to all jj arguments. Complete the environment registry and one clearly defined configuration entry point first, then observe whether the candidates interfere with existing file and command completion. If they do, roll back the shared entry point first rather than mixing the two candidate types back into one action. Still unconfirmed: where the static key set should be maintained, and who decides when to stop completion after the editor command has been tokenized.

Two early directions left in this proposal can still mislead later changes. First, the initial draft treated "being able to find jj" as a reason to enable environment variable candidates as well; it did not specify the types of the candidate values themselves. Second, the initial draft discussed dotted-key discovery and the environment variable registry in the same implementation round, as though they shared a data source. Scanning local configuration files was originally proposed because it seemed like a natural way to obtain dotted keys. This approach was never implemented: configuration files only reflect settings already written on a particular machine, not the set of accepted keys; candidates would also change with the working directory. This section remains to explain why old notes suggest "reading key names from files." That was an option at the time, not the direction now.

Another old approach was to share one action across all arguments that might relate to configuration. It reduced strings at call sites but collapsed two distinct input stages: path arguments started receiving key names, and editor arguments started receiving file candidates. v2 already marked this approach for withdrawal. It remains here because some old entry points may still be found by searching for "shared action"; when you encounter one, first check whether the argument needs a path, a command, or a configuration key. Do not wire it back to the same candidate set just because the names are similar.

`pkg/actions/fs/extension.go` was once used as a starting point for investigation. It does help trace code adjacent to file completion, but it cannot determine where the registry belongs, nor does it establish that dotted keys come from the filesystem. This misreading persisted in the old discussion for a long time: file completion is the value shape needed for a configuration location, not the source of configuration keys.

The environment variable registry rules should be pinned down first. Its purpose is to expose a small set of variables with clear semantics in the command tree when the jj executable is available, not to list every name in the environment. Configuration locations and editors do not share value completion either, because one input ultimately points to a file while the other forms a command line. The earlier wording, "handle each variable separately," was too weak. The constraints are now:

> The guarded jj environment registry must expose JJ_CONFIG as 'The location of the jj config file' with file completion and JJ_EDITOR as 'The default editor' with split command completion whenever the jj executable is available.

This requirement replaces the v1 idea of "display first, then let the caller filter." Callers should not have to infer from the candidate list which action to use for a variable's value; the description and completion shape supplied by the registry should already match the variable. When the executable is unavailable, the old registry should not leave a partial set of candidates behind, especially not names without the corresponding value completion.

This does not make dotted configuration keys an adjunct to the environment variable registry. The trial scope remains narrower here: offer key names only when an argument explicitly interprets its input as a configuration key; keep the existing candidates for path and command arguments. This old proposal has not settled the source for enumerating keys. A static set and a runtime source remain two distinct options; key enumeration must not be forcibly wired into the registry just to reuse it.

The trade-offs between the two options are somewhat clearer now. A static set is predictable and suitable for first validating hierarchical behavior after a dot, but it needs maintenance as keys change; a runtime source is more likely to reflect the settings actually available, but it brings differences in user configuration, directories, and default layers into completion. The earlier test of "the configuration file exists" as evidence that "the key is available" has been discarded. If a runtime source is chosen later, at minimum confirm that the names it returns are accepted at the actual configuration entry point, rather than merely confirming that the read succeeded.

One input question remains unresolved: should top-level candidates provide complete dotted names all at once, or provide top-level segments first and expand further after a dot is entered? The old draft favored a hierarchy because the list was shorter; that preference has not received enough feedback from real entry points to become a fixed rule. If full keys and hierarchical candidates appear together, prioritize avoiding duplicate candidates rather than forcing both versions to remain just to display the hierarchy.

The suggested rollout is also smaller than in the old draft: first wire up the environment registry and check that the two variables' value candidates do not get swapped; then choose one argument that explicitly accepts configuration keys to try dotted-key behavior. Do not start by attaching key names to every argument near configuration. If key names displace path candidates, the editor no longer allows further arguments to be entered, or variable names still appear without jj, roll back the corresponding integration point for any of these failures.

This page still does not fully specify how dotted keys are enumerated, and it retains the abandoned file-scanning direction. It is useful for explaining why the old entry points split into two paths; when adding support for new keys, start at the argument position that actually accepts the key rather than copying a generic list from here.

# Migration Procedure for Revision Files and Logs

In 2023, files, cat, and Log revision changes were first put on the same review page. They all involved revision as an input, but at the time we hadn't confirmed whether it occupied the same position in each command. The old investigation led from the issue name and call name to `pkg/actions/tools/cargo/clippy/clippy.go`; the file header shows `package clippy` and `import (`. Keep this location as a starting point for reading.

The initial split was simple: files would look for paths based on the input so far, while cat would wait for revision before continuing to look for content-related paths. When revision was empty, path completion was temporarily withheld to avoid presenting candidates from the current directory as content from a specified version. This was only the working approach at the time; we hadn't checked whether an empty value had other branches.

During migration, first distinguish revision from path text, then check each command's existing usage, and only then look at where the candidates come from. For Log revision changes, keep just this reminder: finishing the file-path cleanup does not mean the logs have recorded changes to revision.

# Revision Files and Log Migration Workflow

When this page was reorganized for the second time, the short note from 2023 was kept. It explains why files, cat, and Log revision changes were originally grouped together: all the issues involved the word revision, but its position in the command input hadn't been checked first. The old investigation entry point still points to `pkg/actions/tools/cargo/clippy/clippy.go`, with `package clippy` and `import (` visible in the file header. Here, it is only an entry point for reviewing the old notes.

## Earlier Breakdown

The earlier judgment was that files could continue looking for paths based on the current input, while cat had to wait until the revision was clear before proceeding to retrieve content paths. An empty revision was once described as "no path completion," to prevent candidates from the current directory from being mistaken for results under a specified revision. That wasn't a fully verified conclusion about behavior, just a more conservative approach at the time.

Looking back later, two issues had been collapsed into one "empty value": the user not having finished entering the revision and the command having no path source are not the same thing. files might already contain path text, while cat might still be waiting for the content location. The candidate list alone also doesn't show whether a path comes from the current object or another version.

The margin sketch at the time read:

```text
files  -> paths in the current input
cat    -> retrieve content paths after seeing a revision
empty revision -> no path candidates
log    -> add notes separately
```

Keep this sketch for now. It describes the order of operations in 2023, not steps that should continue to be followed later.

## Attempt to change only cat

During the cleanup, we tried a smaller approach: centralize revision handling on the cat side while files continued using the old source for paths. The scope was small, but the maintenance page quickly acquired two interpretations. With the same input still missing a completed revision, the files side looked as if it was using the current object, while the cat side looked as if it was missing a parameter.

This approach was not adopted. It does not prove that files and cat must use the same input format; it only shows that the two commands cannot independently decide where the same revision comes from. The old approach remains here to make it easier to identify later records that still say "cat changed, files unchanged."

That round left one conservative direction: process the revision first, then discuss path candidates; the commands still accept input according to their respective already-public usage. The final handling of an empty revision was not decided in this version.

## Review side note

One side note from the review: path candidates need an owner first; only then does the candidate count have meaning. This is a reminder about checking order, not an interface definition. It does not say that all commands must wait for the revision to be filled in, nor that seeing a path means the revision can be skipped.

When maintaining the old documentation, first state clearly whether the subject is files or cat, then state whether the revision is an explicit value, text awaiting input, or an empty value, and finally record where the path candidates were understood to come from. Keeping only one candidate list is not enough; the list itself cannot explain its source.

## Logs noted separately

`Log revision changes` was initially just one line at the bottom of the page. The file side focuses on how path candidates are obtained, while the logging side focuses on whether the record captured changes to the revision. The two will be brought together through the same issue entry, but the file side appearing normal cannot fill in runtime records for the log.

Someone once suggested that once the wording for files and cat was aligned, the log documentation would naturally follow. That proposal was not adopted. Consistent documentation can reduce misreadings, but it cannot supply missing inputs and outputs. Subsequent cleanup separated file-path verification from log evidence, leaving gaps where the log evidence was insufficient.

## Provisional migration order

When updating old pages, first find sentences that describe files as "getting paths from the current directory," then check whether they place revision handling after the candidates. Next, find sentences that describe cat as "interpreting revision on its own" and check whether it still uses a different source from files. If there are fewer candidates after the change, first record the command, whether revision is empty, whether the path text already exists, and the explanation of where the candidates came from; do not immediately restore the old list.

For a partial rollback, restore the affected old documentation or candidate source, rather than treating "always stop when revision is empty" as the answer again. Do not rewrite the log documentation along with the file-side rollback; without new records, it remains marked as unconfirmed.

Two items remain open: the fallback target for an empty revision in files; and which page will maintain the conflicting descriptions in the log evidence over the long term.

# Migration workflow for revision files and logs

This page started as a record of path completion for files and cat, and was later used to track older descriptions of Log revision changes. It has never been rewritten from scratch. The first half still contains several rounds of notes from different periods: some were meant to keep candidates from misleading users; others came after reviews revealed that changing only one side would give the same revision two different meanings. The criteria to use when checking the migration are at the end of the page.

File paths and log records have always been treated separately. The file side needs to answer which selected version the candidates belong to; the log side needs to answer whether the material records changes to revision. Both can be found through the same entry point, but when one side has no results, text from the other side cannot be used to fill the gap.

## The starting point in 2023: avoid misleading users first

The initial notes addressed a straightforward case: the user's input already contains path text, but revision is not yet complete. If the page first shows paths from the current directory, readers may interpret those candidates as paths in the specified version. So the early notes described files as path-first and cat as content-first; when revision was empty, path completion was withheld.

The original short note is retained below:

> files first looks for paths based on the current input; cat fetches content once it sees revision. When revision is empty, hold off on path completion to avoid bringing in candidates from the current directory.

That note had context from the situation at the time, but left two things unaddressed. It did not distinguish between "the user is still entering revision" and "the command has no available source of paths," nor did it explain how cat gets paths once revision is present. In the even earlier records, there were no samples to check whether candidates came from the current directory, a selected version, or results left over from the previous lookup.

Log revision changes appear only once, at the end of the page. That line is only a reminder to check later whether the log materials describe revision changes as ordinary path changes; it must not be read as a log check that has already been completed.

## On-call margin note from the same year

A sentence was added next to the on-call record: do not first construct a path from the current directory and then add a revision explanation to the path. It concerns the order, not "an empty value always stops." However, the person who wrote this sentence did not decide where an empty revision goes, so the old rule remains on the same page.

Someone later read the margin note as "all candidates have to wait until revision is filled in." That is not a conclusion it supports. It only requires clarifying the path's ownership first, then explaining when candidates appear. The early pages did not spell out this distinction, so some maintenance records continued using the stop branch, while others used the existing path text directly.

The old sketch was not deleted either:

```text
2023 year sketch (deprecated)

files  ──> path in the current input
cat    ──> content path after discovering revision
revision is empty ──> provide no path candidates
log materials       ──> review after file-side confirmation
```

The problem with this diagram is not that it is short, but that it has no shared revision selection point. The last line also places the logs after the file side, which makes it easy to think that a normal file path is enough to account for log behavior. That relationship was later retracted, but the old diagram remains as a historical trace.

## 2024 year: Splitting the input

The second pass did not immediately replace the old paragraphs. Instead, it split the two commands' inputs into two kinds of text: revision text and path text. This exposed differences that the command names had previously obscured. The same empty revision could accompany a path that had already been entered, or it could leave only an input with no content location yet.

This pass did not produce a complete behavior specification; it settled only the migration order: stop letting files and cat each decide where the revision comes from. Identify the revision selection first, then look at path candidates. This order does not mean the two commands must accept the same format, nor does it mean every empty value must produce candidates.

One question mark on the review sheet remained unerased: when path text is present but the revision is unfinished, should files candidates be treated as pending input, or as paths in some default object? This version did not pretend that was settled. The old "stop on empty values" rule cannot answer it either, because it only describes the motivation to avoid misleading users.

The same pass revisited the old investigation entry point and still recorded `pkg/actions/tools/cargo/clippy/clippy.go`. The `package clippy` and `import (` at the top of the file can help readers get back to the file from the old issue name, but that location itself cannot replace verification of files, cat, or the log material. The path comes from a navigation record for an old revision; it does not establish that implementation ownership has changed.

## An approach that did not work out

A small change affecting only cat was proposed at the time. cat would centralize revision handling, while files would keep its original path source. On the surface, only one place needed changing. Once this was written into the maintenance notes, however, two similar inputs led to two different interpretations: files appeared to be using the current object, while cat appeared to be missing an argument.

This approach was not adopted. It was removed not because cat should not handle revision, but because changing only cat would let files continue to bypass the selection process that must be checked against. The old paragraph is retained, with the marker from that time added:

> Deprecated: Adding revision only on the cat side still leaves files obtaining candidates from the old path source.

When a report says "cat has changed, files has not," compare it with this transition period first. Do not treat the old approach as two optional paths, and do not judge whether the migration succeeded based only on the number of candidates. Candidates appearing or disappearing only shows that the list changed; by itself, it does not prove that the candidates came from the correct revision.

After this failure, a local stop point was added: if we cannot explain which revision the path comes from, the files-side migration must not be recorded as complete. This stop point constrains path candidates only; it cannot be used to declare Log revision changes verified.

## Debate left by the review

In one review, someone argued that writing the handling of `--revision` in a shared location would be sufficient. Another view pointed out that shared terminology still cannot explain when the path is obtained; even if the two commands are written in the same section, they may obtain candidates from different locations.

The review excerpt is retained as:

> The path's provenance comes first; only then does the number of candidates mean anything. Writing revision in the same section is not enough to explain where the candidates come from.

This sentence is not an interface definition. It only explains why the page continues to ask at which step selection occurs and at which step the path appears. The review also required that gaps in the logs not be used to fill in examples for files or cat. Therefore, this page retains the relationship between the two entry points, but does not present the logs as verification results for the files side.

Another old opinion was that "once the wording is aligned, the logs will naturally follow." No actionable evidence was left to support that opinion, and it was later treated as a shortcut that no longer applied. Without supporting material, the log description should still remain unconfirmed, rather than borrowing the apparently normal candidate list from the file side.

## Close out file paths and log material separately

On the file-path side, the checks cover revision, command usage, and candidate sources. On the log side, they cover the present wording of Log revision changes and whether it has inputs, outputs, or a location where records are stored. Both contain the word revision, so the old page tended to connect them into a single pipeline; in actual maintenance, completing the former cannot produce records for the latter.

The old page placed logs under "look at this after confirming the file side." That layout was a temporary sequence from 2023; it is retained so that old issue reports remain readable, not to define a dependency. A review today should first address the relationship between revision and paths in file commands, then check the log material independently; if the log material is insufficient, keep the unconfirmed items open.

This also explains why this page does not treat the candidate table as final evidence. A candidate list can at most show results; it cannot establish whether those results came from the current directory, the selected revision, or a temporary cache. If the log wording also reuses the old path explanation, readers will mistake a file migration for a change in log behavior.

## Card entry points from 2025

JJC-204's local description requires confirming in a real CI run whether Revision-aware files and cat paths take effect; the presence of config files cannot substitute for runtime results. After the existing implementation was reviewed, the work was handed to the current module maintainer and then moved into progress. This page therefore records "has an implementation entry point" and "has runtime confirmation" separately.

JJC-210 handles the missing runtime record for Log revision changes. The card later included a correction: one item there is still unconfirmed, and the inputs and outputs for this one remain in the candidate filtering matrix. This only indicates that a gap remains on the logging side; it does not provide a final result that can be inferred. The candidate lists for files or cat cannot answer for it.

Each card retains one navigation entry. JJC-204 points to the runtime check for the file paths; JJC-210 points to the log wording and that unconfirmed item. The cards do not replace the rules on this page, nor does either card cover the other item.

## Three outdated interpretations to set aside before migration

The first old interpretation is "files is a path command, so revision doesn't matter." It treats the path text as a self-contained object and misses which version the candidate ultimately belongs to. The second is "cat has revision, so handle it only on the cat side." This gives the same revision term different origins next to the two commands.

The third treats an unfilled revision directly as invalid input and terminates. This came from an earlier approach to prevent candidates from the current directory from being mixed in, but it did not first distinguish the command's public usage from the input position. When maintaining old material, first mark whether you are checking files or cat; then state whether revision is an explicit value, text awaiting input, or an empty value; finally record which object the candidate should belong to. If any one of the three is unclear, stop at the old paragraph instead of substituting the candidate count for an explanation.

Here, "stop" only means not yet marking the migration as complete; it does not mean deleting the old record. The old record still needs to be retained because it explains why the page once handled empty values so conservatively.

## Current Migration Entry Point

The current handling no longer has the two commands look for the source of revision separately. First, return to each command's documented usage and identify where revision and the path occur in the input; then make revision selection happen before the path candidates; finally, check whether the candidates come from the selected object. files and cat can still retain their respective usages, but they cannot each find a separate source for the same revision.

The current verification sentence remains in the original wording: The files and cat commands must use their documented usages, resolve --revision through the shared revision action, and obtain path candidates from the selected revision, using @ when the files revision is empty.

This sentence replaces the earlier split in which "files looked at the current input, while cat obtained a separate revision," and makes 2024's "select first, then obtain paths" concrete as three checks: command usage, the shared revision action, and the source of candidates from the selected revision. The final @ applies only when the files revision is empty. The old paragraph does not include these qualifications and must not be used alongside this one.

During migration, review files' documented usages first, then cat's documented usages. This reading order is only to keep the two commands from being conflated; it does not mean files has higher priority than cat. After confirming the input positions for both sides, check whether `--revision` has gone through the shared revision action. If either side still determines the revision independently, do not compare its candidates with the other side's.

Then inspect the candidate sources. Candidates must be obtained from the selected revision; do not retrieve them first from the current directory or the old temporary path table and then add a revision explanation afterward. When the files revision is empty, use @ as the fallback, then obtain the paths from the selected revision. The page does not require @ to be displayed as user-visible text, but the maintenance record must not write the empty value as "no revision".

The empty-value branch for cat cannot simply copy files. The current wording specifies @ only for files; cat still enters the shared revision action according to its own documented usages. If an old description writes cat's empty value as the same branch as files, go back and verify cat's usage instead of merging the two handling paths for visual symmetry.

The sequence is:

```text
Old fragmented path (deprecated)

files ──> path candidates
cat   ──> revision check ──> path candidates

Current path

files ─┐
       ├─> documented usages ─> shared revision action ─> selected revision ─> path candidates
cat   ┘

files revision is empty ─> @ ─> selected revision ─> path candidates
```

The change in the diagram is not to show files and cat as taking the same input, but to place path candidates after selected revision. If either side obtains paths before revision selection, first review that side's inputs and documented usages; don't mask the ordering issue by changing the candidate-filtering wording.

## Migrating the Old Description

When updating an old page, you can start with individual sentences.

- Change sentences that describe files as "current directory paths" to first verify its own documented usages, then state that the paths are obtained after selected revision.
- Change sentences that describe cat as "interpreting revision on its own" to check the shared revision action; don't just remove the revision wording next to cat and make the selection action disappear.
- Keep the sentence "stop if revision is empty" in the historical section, mark it as deprecated next to files' current section, and add the @ fallback.
- Adjust the diagram that lists paths first and explains revision later so that selected revision appears first, followed by path candidates.
- Split apart sentences that describe Log revision changes as a files-side result; logs should continue to be described using their own source material.

After migration, if unexpected candidates appear, first ask whether they come from selected revision. If not, the issue is still before revision selection; don't change the candidate filtering first. If the candidates do come from selected revision, review the documented usages of files or cat separately. This distinguishes a source-ordering issue from a problem with the command's own usage.

A targeted restore is used to retract a single migration statement, not to reinstate the old guidance. First restore the affected command's original documented usages, then confirm that `--revision` still goes through the shared revision action. Do not move path retrieval ahead of selection just to make candidates appear again.

When the revision for files is empty, keep the @ fallback after the restore. The old page's wording, "stop on an empty value," records a concern from that time, not behavior that can be re-enabled. Restoring cat must not borrow the empty-value branch from files either; restore cat's own documented usages, then continue through the shared action.

There is no shortcut to restoring the log side through file paths. If the description of Log revision changes is retracted, restore only the previously confirmed wording and retain the unconfirmed items. Do not write that logs have also been restored just because file candidates are working correctly.

## Items still set aside

The gap in the candidate filtering matrix identified by JJC-210 remains set aside as a separate item. What can be confirmed is that it relates to conflicting descriptions of Log revision changes; the inputs and outputs have not been filled in on this page. If supporting material is found later, put it back on the log side first, then decide whether the migration notes need to change. Do not feed a log record back in as evidence of files or cat behavior.

Older material may still contain comments that describe @ as the "current directory." This related issue has no separate record. If it turns up again, first determine whether it appears in the empty-revision branch of files or in a general path description, then handle each occurrence individually. The fact that the current wording already specifies where @ belongs does not justify replacing all old comments in one pass.

Another item that has not been split out is the old investigation entry point. `pkg/actions/tools/cargo/clippy/clippy.go` can still be used to look back at early issue names and call names, but its file location does not carry all the migration judgments on this page. If an old record is reached through that path again, return to the three areas—command usage, revision selection, and candidate sources—rather than treating the path itself as a conclusion.

## Handling guidance retained after review

The review did not ask for this page to become a complete command reference. It only required the current section to be distinguishable from the old approach: old paragraphs retain their time context, and the current section appears later; file candidates must not be used to fill gaps in the logs; the empty-revision fallback for files must not be overridden by the handling for cat.

A record of a completed migration therefore needs to show at least three local facts: which command is being examined, where revision selection is entered, and whether path candidates appear before or after that selection. A list of paths alone, or just the words "aligned," is still not enough to replace the old record. No separate run-results table is being added here, because the run checks for JJC-204 and the log gaps for JJC-210 belong under their respective entry points.

This section reflects maintenance guidance added later and must not be backdated to the year 2023. At the time, the early authors only knew how to avoid misleading candidates; they did not know how to write the later shared actions and @ fallback. The old paragraphs remain for identifying them when looking up old issues and should not be polished into current steps.

## Appendix: Old quick-handling method (no longer applicable)

The section below was once copied into on-call notes and is retained for identifying early pages. It is not part of the current migration steps.

```text
1. If files has a path, fill it in from the current directory.
2. Only consider the path when cat shows revision.
3. If revision is not written, do not fill it in, to avoid guessing wrong.
4. When there is no log record, check whether the reference-file side is functioning normally.
```

Steps 1 and 2 split up the revision selection; step 3 ignored the @ fallback for an empty revision in files; step 4 mistakenly treated log verification as an adjunct to file-path verification. They remain because old issue reports may continue to use these terms, not because they are valid alongside the current entry point.

Another older diagram places path candidates before revision. If you encounter the same layout, treat it as an earlier migration stage: there is no need to delete the history, but path retrieval should be moved after selected revision, and the documented usages of files and cat should each be reviewed.

# Ancestor and descendant offset trial-run notes

These notes keep two easily conflated topics in JJ-2026.09 separate: the revision selector's ancestor/descendant offsets, and regression observations for Obslog revision and tool. For the former, start with how candidates are presented in `prev` and `next`; the latter remains a separate entry point awaiting a run.

The source review reference is recorded at `completers/jj_completer/cmd/prev.go`. It was not treated as the Obslog implementation location at the time; it was only a starting point for checking candidate order, description text, and usage hints on the prev side. The available material does not include a rerunnable command, environment, or output, so these notes do not reconstruct results from an undocumented run.

The original experiment had a narrow scope: use the same set of revision inputs to inspect ancestor and descendant offset candidates, and record whether the current commit appears among the candidates, how the numbers are displayed, and whether description fields are preserved. The Obslog path must not use these observations as its conclusions.

During review, the criterion used in the notes was: The prev and next commands must expose zero-padded ancestor or descendant offsets, exclude the current commit, preserve commit descriptions, and keep the next usage 'next [OPTIONS] [AMOUNT]'.

This criterion filled a gap in the early notes: they only said "look at the revisions before and after," without separating offset display from the requirement to exclude the current commit. # Chmod Path Position Troubleshooting Tree

This page was originally used to troubleshoot completion issues with Chmod mode and path positions. The old notes split the symptoms quickly: first ask whether mode appeared, then put any blanks, duplicates, or misalignment after it into the path branch. That was convenient when taking notes on the spot, but on review it made it easy to mix up "what we saw" with "where we thought it belonged."

The tree from the first draft is still here. It reflects the troubleshooting approach used at the time, not the behavior established by later review.

```text
Mode visible
├─ No further candidates appear → Treat as missing path
└─ Candidates still appear      → Treat as a path position offset

Mode not visible
└─ Treat as missing mode; do not investigate path further
```

The first problem with this tree is that it treats mode being visible first as a prerequisite every time. The second is that it calls all subsequent input path, so it did not capture the relationship between the cursor position at the time, the input already entered, and the candidates displayed. The statement in the old notes, "once mode appears, check path first," should be treated as an outdated working hypothesis. It is retained because people still use this entry point to find old screenshots and descriptions.

When collecting observations now, do not name the issue yet. First make a pair of calls that can be compared: one successful call and one failed call. Save the visible results for both, especially which part the user had entered up to, whether the list appeared, the first entries in the list, and what changed on screen as they continued typing. The local instructions for JJC-208 also call for saving results from these two calls, not for inferring the cause from the list first.

## Capture It As Is Before Choosing a Branch

Once you have the report, follow the sequence below. At each step, address only what is observed there; if the required evidence is missing, stop at that step rather than filling the gap with a conclusion.

```text
Start
│
├─ Do you have both a successful invocation and a failed invocation?
│  ├─ No: Add a comparison pair and record the text entered and the on-screen results; stop here
│  └─ Yes: Continue
│
├─ Are both invocations at the same input position?
│  ├─ No: Record an input position mismatch; do not classify it as mode or path; stop here
│  └─ Yes: Continue
│
├─ Did mode-related candidates appear first in the successful invocation?
│  ├─ Yes: Save that view alongside the same position in the failed invocation
│  └─ No: Do not carry over the old tree's "missing mode" conclusion; look at the original screen from the failed invocation instead
│
├─ Does the failed invocation still show candidates?
│  ├─ No: Record "no candidates"; do not write it up as a missing path
│  └─ Yes: Continue
│
└─ Do the candidates in the failed invocation appear at the same input position as in the successful invocation?
   ├─ Yes: Record the differences in candidate content and input position, and wait for review
   └─ No: Record the position change and wait for review
```

"Same input position" here does not simply mean the command names match. It means both invocations are stopped at the position where the user wants completion, and the text already entered can be checked side by side. If one stops before mode and the other after it, they cannot be treated as the same sample, even if both contain the same words. The old page folded this distinction into the path branch, leaving later questions with nothing but "the path is wrong" and no way to reconstruct what happened.

If the successful invocation shows candidates and the failing invocation shows none, save the full visible lines from both. Do not add "therefore mode completion did not finish" or "therefore path completion did not finish" to the record. No candidates describes only the screen state; it does not, by itself, show how far candidate generation got or which rules were used to interpret the input position.

If the failing invocation still shows candidates, the old procedure would immediately check whether they were paths. Use that check only to find older material now: put the failing list and the successful list side by side and compare where they appear. If the list contents are similar but their positions differ, record the position difference; if the positions are the same but the contents differ, record the content difference; if both differ, record each difference. Do not use "misalignment" as a catch-all for these three cases.

## Scope of the old branches

Not every step in the old tree is useless. It can help provisionally sort legacy reports into three buckets: no mode seen, mode seen but no candidates after it, and mode seen with candidates still appearing after it. This grouping helps with lookup, but should no longer determine the order of fixes.

- If a report only says "there's nothing to complete," the old tree would place it under either missing mode or missing path. Ask for the input position first instead; without a position, do not pick a bucket.
- If a report provides only one candidate list, the old tree would treat the list as evidence of path. Mark it as a one-sided sample instead; it cannot be compared with a successful invocation.
- If a report provides both successful and failing screens, but the text already entered differs between the two, the old tree might still describe the latter as a shift in the path position. Treat this as a non-comparable pair and stop there first.
- If a report says "mode is normal, path is abnormal" without explaining where mode appeared, retain the original wording, but do not rewrite it as a judgment about the implementation.

These stopping points are deliberately earlier than those in the old record. They do not resolve the Chmod completion issue; they only prevent on-call notes from producing more specific, incorrect conclusions without a comparison. The old account treated missing candidates and candidates appearing in the wrong position as one continuous failure chain; the available material does not support that continuity.

## Review entry point

The old record ultimately pointed to `completers/golangci-lint_completer/cmd/config_path.go`. This does not prove where Chmod behavior is defined; it is only the file entry point left from following the issue name and call name at the time. The top of that file directly shows `package cmd` and `import (`; beyond those, this page contains no excerpts of declarations sufficient to determine the mode or path rules.

When opening that path, do only two things: confirm that you are viewing the version material referenced by the old record; copy local excerpts that map directly to the success and failure screenshots into the investigation notes. If all you see are similarly named symbols, do not reclassify the report on that basis. Similar names were precisely why the old tree was trusted too much.

Related cards JJC-208 collect the findings from this entry-point investigation. Later public comments on the cards retain the status "one point unconfirmed"; this is not a completion marker. If new material only repeats the old screenshots without adding side-by-side results for successful and failing calls, keep "unconfirmed." Do not narrow the issue just because the cards have moved into an active work status.

## On-call note format

The format below replaces the single line "check path" on the old page. Stop at the first field you cannot confirm; you do not need to establish the cause first.

```text
Symptom title:
Successful invocation: content entered / position stopped at / candidates visible on screen
Failed invocation: content entered / position stopped at / candidates visible on screen
Are the two comparable: yes / no
Difference: different positions / different content / both different / no candidates
Legacy branch used:
Unconfirmed points:
```

"Legacy branch used" is only there to keep old reports searchable. You can enter missing mode, missing path, or position offset here, but this does not establish a cause. If there isn't enough on-screen evidence to judge, enter "undetermined"; don't pick one of the three legacy branches just to complete the form.

## Deprecated recovery actions

The old version recommended shifting attention to path as soon as mode appeared and treating subsequent input as being in the path position. This recovery action no longer applies. It causes the person investigating to skip the corresponding position in the successful invocation and to record "candidates still present" and "candidates outside the expected position" as the same symptom.

Another old recommendation was not to go back and check mode when the failed invocation had no candidates. This recommendation is also retained but not used. A screen with no candidates cannot prove what happened at the previous position; at minimum, compare it with the visible result of the successful invocation before recording it.

If a legacy ticket has already been handled using the old recommendations, only add a new comparison description; do not overwrite the original classification. The original classification shows which branch of the tree the investigator followed at the time; the new description fills in the input position and screen result that were missing then. Keeping both records is more useful than rewriting the old wording to make it sound as though those details were already known at the time.

## Still stuck on

There is currently no material that establishes a fixed ordering between `mode` and path positions, nor any material showing that the result from a single screen is sufficient to determine where the anomaly is. JJC-208 records a review focused on the visible results of one successful call and one failed call; beyond this comparison, this page does not extend to other command positions or other completion entry points.

When a new sample arrives, first check whether it provides the input positions for both sides. If it does not, state in "Unconfirmed" whether the missing information is the successful call, the failed call, or the position description. If it does, use the tree to distinguish between no candidates, different content, and different positions. Do not backfill conclusions from the old tree, and do not treat a file path as completed localization.
