# Branch Completion Compatibility Migration Procedure

The old records have long led people from branch-related issue names to `completers/git_completer/cmd/filterBranch.go`. This entry point has not been removed: it is still useful for comparing the old call names, candidate lists, and local filtering side by side. The file belongs to the `cmd` package, and the only visible neighboring reference at the top of the file is `import (`. Early records therefore gave it a lot of weight, as though it could fully explain both the branch lifecycle and remote fetching.

This document has not been rewritten into a new, unified account. It preserves a migration record: the old investigation path led from call names to `filterBranch.go`, while later compatibility checks require the two topics to be kept separate. The old path is still useful, especially for recovering the candidates compared at the time; it is no longer enough to replace an independent review of each topic.

## Using the Old Entry Point

The original migration goal was not to replace a known implementation, but to keep reviewers from having to guess again where branch filtering sits in the command tree. The recorded sequence was: first, use the words branch, state, completion, list, set, use, and local in the issue to get back to the old call names; then open `completers/git_completer/cmd/filterBranch.go`; finally, compare the old candidate output with the target version's output side by side.

The assessment at the time was that branch lifecycle completion and Fetch remote branches could be checked along the same path. That assessment remains here because the early notes, rollback discussions, and call names were all organized around it. It later proved insufficiently accurate, but it was not entirely without value: both types of issue do lead investigators back to the same old entry point. The problem is that starting from the same entry point does not mean the differences in both areas should be explained by the same state, the same set of inputs, or the same recovery action.

```text
Early record
Issue name / invocation name
        |
        v
completers/git_completer/cmd/filterBranch.go
        |
        +-----------------------------+
        |                             |
        v                             v
Branch-lifecycle candidate       Remote-branch fetch candidate
        |                             |
        +-------- Historical merge record --------+

Follow-up verification
The old entry point is for navigation only
        |
        +--> JJC-209: platform and version in the configuration
        |
        +--> JJC-220: syntax changes in the current version
```

The "Follow-up verification" section above is not a code-path diagram. It only shows where the old record should be taken for further investigation: the entry file brings the reader back to the local context at the time; the cards separately record the objects that still need to be confirmed. Combining the two cards into a single "branch issue" would reintroduce the old misreading of the record.

## Branch-switching steps at the time

The early procedure kept two sets of artifacts. The first contains the input that originally triggered the issue and its completion candidates; keeping only the conclusion that "there is a difference" is not enough. The second contains the same input and its output on the target version. With the two sets side by side, first mark which candidates were added or removed, then decide whether to investigate further by following `filterBranch.go`. The old records do not list the full call relationships, so the filename is not identified here as the only place to change.

The old sequence has a practical benefit: it lets you fall back to a familiar candidate list first, rather than changing branch-state filtering as soon as a difference appears. In early investigations, "local branches," "completed status," and "remote names" often appeared in the same set of terms. Changing them all at once would make it impossible to tell later which condition changed the candidates.

But the old sequence was also misleading. Checking the branch lifecycle requires first looking at which platforms and versions the current build configuration covers; checking Fetch remote branches requires running the source code from the report unchanged on the current version and marking the specific syntactic units that changed. They can share the old output as a reference, but they should not share the same "verified" flag.

The following manual sequence can still be retained during migration:

1. Retain the old inputs, candidates, and entry points; do not replace them with new descriptions.
2. First decide whether you are checking lifecycle behavior or remote fetching; if both appear, split them into two records.
3. For lifecycle items, start with the build configuration, list the platforms and versions already covered, and tie each gap to a specific configuration file.
4. For remote-fetching items, run the source code from the report unchanged on the current version and mark the syntax units that have changed.
5. If the output differs from the old record, save the differences first, then consider inspecting filtering adjacency through the old entry point.

"Migration" here means migrating records and review entry points, not requiring `filterBranch.go` to be replaced with a new file. The old file remains in place; it just no longer serves as the basis for every conclusion.

## The branch lifecycle track

The observation left by JJC-209 is narrow: Branch lifecycle completion behaves abnormally under a particular usage pattern. The work item on the card requires checking the platforms and versions involved against the current build configuration and tying each gap to a specific configuration file. This requirement changes the starting point used in the old records. Previously, looking only at the candidate list made it easy to misreport a platform or version gap as a change in filtering logic; now, document the coverage in the build configuration first, then return to comparing candidates.

Records can be organized at the following level of granularity:

| What to retain | What to record |
| --- | --- |
| Original candidates | The full candidate list for the old input, not just the anomalous entries |
| Build configuration | Platforms and versions checked in this round, and combinations not yet seen |
| Location of the difference | Whether the change is in candidate names, state selection, or call timing |
| Old entry point | Whether local filtering needs to be traced again from `filterBranch.go` |

This table does not need to be filled out completely in every round. The old page is still referenced precisely because it preserves the practice of "starting with candidate differences and tracing back to the old entry point." But for JJC-209, platform and version checks must come before attributing the issue to state filtering. Until the configuration scope is documented clearly, candidate changes should not be interpreted as changes to the lifecycle rules themselves.

The record for month 9, day 26 included `rollback_checked`. This means someone checked the fallback path at the time, not that every kind of candidate difference had been resolved or that the item had been fully verified. The reassignment later that day did not establish the cause of the differences either. The old page used to treat these two status updates as supporting evidence that "the migration was stable"; they can now only be retained as a record of the work done at the time.

If these checks require a temporary return to the old path, first restore the old input and old candidates side by side, then remove the assessments added in this round. Do not overwrite it with a different type of branch input. The restored record must still state that it is for Branch lifecycle completion, rather than bringing back the remote-fetch results along with it.

## The Fetch remote branches branch

JJC-220 has a different starting point. The card requires running the source code from the Fetch remote branches report unchanged on the current version and circling the specific syntax units that have changed. The primary deliverables here are not a generalized table of branch candidates, but the unchanged source code, the current execution result, and the circled syntax locations. If the candidate list also changes, it can be appended, but candidate changes cannot replace the syntax check.

For this migration path, start with the source code saved in the report. Do not rewrite it from memory into an "equivalent" form; equivalence is precisely what cannot be assumed here. After execution, record the result from the current version right next to the unchanged source code, then mark which syntax units no longer match the original report. If you need to inspect the old filtering adjacency, you can still open `completers/git_completer/cmd/filterBranch.go`, but it is only a reference point for looking back.

The addendum for month 10 explicitly left one point unconfirmed. It did not say whether that point should be classified as a remote-name difference, a branch-state difference, or some other parsing difference, so do not fill it in as a known implementation conclusion. The old page's practice was to mark both Fetch remote branches and the lifecycle item as passed as soon as any one difference could be reproduced; that practice no longer applies. At a minimum, the record should keep the unconfirmed point separate: it belongs with the unchanged source code and syntax annotations, not with the build configuration checklist for JJC-209.

The recovery steps for this branch also differ. If running the current version as-is does not allow the comparison to continue, first undo this round of syntax-unit annotations and retain the source code from the original report and the output already obtained; do not rewrite it as a general description of the remote inventory. Only if the filtered candidates differ from the old results should the old entry point be used for the next lookup. This prevents a single unexplained execution result from causing all remote-branch candidates to be misclassified as rollback targets.

## Old plan and where it is retained

The old plan put both items into one migration batch for a simple reason: both led from branch terminology back to the same piece of local code. Later work split this plan into separate tracks, but it remains on the page. Some people still find this page through the old call names; removing it would leave the early candidate outputs without a reference point.

When retaining the old plan, add a correction alongside it: a shared entry point only means that tracing back can start from the same place; verification of Branch lifecycle completion starts with the build configuration, while verification of Fetch remote branches starts by preserving the source code as-is and the syntax differences. This correction is enough to change the order of operations; there is no need to invent a complete dependency relationship between the two objects.

JJC-209 and JJC-220 are navigation entry points for the follow-up records. DOC-21 retains another set of verification objects; its directories, operation history, or conflict-path results must not be used to fill the gaps in these two items.

## Gaps still left at the bottom of the page

- JJC-220's unconfirmed item has not yet been categorized here.
- The missing platform and version in JJC-209 need to be mapped to specific configuration files before the differences among the old candidates can be revisited.
- The old fallback check did not specify its coverage; do not use it to broaden the recovery conclusions.

This page retains the old entry point, the old merge assessment, and the subsequent split order for those who need to trace back early branch issues.

In JJ-2026.09, "Merge and move sources" and "Squash changed paths" will initially be recorded as two independent requirements tracks. Both fall under completion scenarios after changes, but having change-related words in both names is not grounds for treating them as the same issue.

# Decision Record: Sources and Paths After Changes

When this page was first written, the discussion covered only two names that were easy to conflate: "Merge and move sources" and "Squash changed paths". Both appeared in completion scenarios after changes, so older records could easily lump them together as a generic "completion issue after changes". At the time, there wasn't enough material from actual calls to establish whether they went through the same filtering point, nor was there any reason to infer identical implementations from similar names.

The original decision did not require two separate implementations for the two scenarios. It required keeping them separate in the records first: after sources move, which source a particular call actually uses; after paths change, which paths remain visible among the candidates. The first question concerns the caller, the actual version, the entry point, and the current result; the second concerns the visible results left by successful and failed calls respectively. The two sides may eventually help explain each other, but until the material is complete, neither can settle the conclusion for the other.

## Classification approaches rejected at the time

One option considered was to create a single "completion after changes" entry and attach the outputs under both names in one place. The benefit was minimal maintenance: each new observation would only need another paragraph. The problem was that once the outputs differed, the record itself could not distinguish whether the difference came from source movement or path selection. A successful path sample would obscure an entry point that had not yet been verified in the source scenario; an issue in the source scenario might also be misrecorded as a general failure of path candidates.

Another option considered was to first pick a seemingly relevant source-code location, then group all observed cases under it. This approach was also rejected. A source-code location can provide a starting point for tracing back, but it does not automatically establish which call accounts for which kind of user-visible result. Treating the location as the cause first would make it easy, when successful and failed path records were added later, to mistake differences between calls for intermittent variation in the same processing layer.

The decision retained is straightforward: archive source-related and path-related material separately; discuss whether to combine attribution only when both sides have actual results that can be compared. This decision governs the order of assessment, not whether code can be shared later. It also keeps unverified implementation relationships out of the requirements history.

## Two leads added after review

JJC-211 brought "inconsistent results for Merge and move sources in the user environment" back for review. The card requires first finding a caller that still uses "Merge and move sources," then checking the actual version, entry point, and present results. This requirement supplies the unit of observation missing from the early records: rather than retaining only an issue name, it ties an active caller to its running version and results.

The card later recorded a QA reproduction action, after which the work moved from To Do to In Progress. Those status changes do not by themselves establish that source movement has been explained; they only show that the issue has entered actual review and can no longer be tracked solely by its initial wording-based classification. The source track still needs to be grounded in that caller's actual version, entry point, and present results, rather than substituting path samples or source-code navigation.

JJC-216 adds a different lead. It records "Squash changed paths regression in the user environment" and requires retaining the visible results from one successful call and one failed call separately. After the risk review, the card still stated, "One point in Squash changed paths remains unconfirmed." This means the path side cannot be recorded as working across the board just because a successful call exists, nor can the follow-up review on the source side be used to fill in the details of the failed call.

The two cards change the level of detail this page should retain, not the existing boundary. JJC-211 show that source scenarios require checking at least the caller, version, entry point, and current result; JJC-216 show that path scenarios require retaining at least the results visible under each of the contrasting calls. The former is not a success condition for the latter, and the latter is not the result of the former's version check.

## Recording approach now in use

| Lead | What this page retains | Not a substitute |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Merge and move sources | Callers still in use, actual versions, entry points, current results | Success or failure samples for Squash changed paths |
| Squash changed paths | Visible results from one successful call and one failed call | Caller version and entry point records for source scenarios |

This is not an acceptance table. It only fixes where the two types of material belong, so that later additions don't treat matching command terms as a causal relationship. The source track answers what result an entry point still in use produces now; the path track answers what the reader actually saw under two contrasting calls. Even if the same candidate terms appear in both types of material, they should still be recorded separately first.

Using two tracks adds a little organizational overhead. Each new piece of material has to be classified first: does it describe the source or the path? But this costs less than keeping a consolidated record. While JJC-216 still has unconfirmed points, a merged success sample would look like an overall conclusion; when JJC-211 needs the actual version confirmed, a path-side failure sample cannot answer which entry point the caller actually got the result from.

We also chose not to wait until all observations were confirmed before recording the decision. Waiting would erase the original distinction, leaving later reviewers to guess from the card titles why the material was not merged. The decision is clear enough: collect separately, describe separately, and do not merge the attribution without shared evidence. Whether the two tracks ultimately lead to the same change is still for later review to determine.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Separate
    state "Record separately" as Separate
    state "Source review" as Source
    state "Path review" as Path
    state "Keep separate" as Keep
    Separate --> Source: Merge and move sources
    Separate --> Path: Squash changed paths
    Source --> Keep: Check caller, version, entry point, and current result
    Path --> Keep: Retain successful and failed results and unconfirmed points
    Keep --> [*]
```

The endpoint in the diagram does not mean the issue is closed. It means that, based on the available material, both tracks lead back to the same decision: keep them separate. The diagram and the classification on this page only need to change if later evidence shows a call or processing relationship that directly connects the two.

## Source code lookup location

The existing navigation points to `completers/kubectl_completer/cmd/set_resources.go`. In the frozen version, `package cmd` and `import (` are directly visible in the file header. This is enough to make it a starting point for examining command-layer adjacency and to anchor the old investigation notes to a fixed path.

This page does not use that path to attribute source or path issues to an implementation. The path alone does not establish the actual version, entry point, or result for the caller of "Merge and move sources," nor does it provide the visible result of the failed call on JJC-216. Treating a navigation location as a common attribution would only repeat an approach already abandoned early on.

If further investigation finds that the two scenarios share a direct call relationship, a cross-reference can be added here; without that material, the path remains a lookup aid only. Local declarations and adjacency in the current revision can help narrow the reading scope, but cannot replace records from the actual cases.

## Retained wording and open items

The original draft said, "If both lines point to the same implementation, revisit combining the handling decisions." That sentence is retained, but it no longer means that combining them is the default. The reviewed material only shows that case-specific evidence is still needed on both sides; it does not establish a shared implementation. The sentence should now be read as a conditional follow-up option: discuss combining them when there is evidence of a direct connection; otherwise, keep the two tracks separate.

On the source side, we still need to verify the versions, entry points, and current results for callers still in use. On the path side, we still need to retain the unconfirmed item and make the visible results of successful and failed calls comparable. During review, first check whether the source track has stable caller results, then whether failures on the path track can still be distinguished from successful samples. Only once we have material for both questions is it worth assessing whether they belong to the same regression.

# Rebase/Diffedit proposal

The old draft put `Rebase revision subsets` and `Diffedit boundary revisions` on the same review sheet simply because both involve revision selection and display. We can keep that starting point, but it created a misleading impression: that the two entry points differ only in where a parameter goes. We no longer use that description. The two names refer to different boundaries, and reusing selection results is still an option, not an agreed interface arrangement.

The source location is unchanged: `completers/jj_completer/cmd/rebase.go`. The terms left there—rebase, revision, destination, branch, source, flags—are search terms for finding that location, not a map of which fields belong where. The `package cmd` at the top of the file and the imports only establish that this is a location adjacent to the command side; they do not give us Diffedit's execution chain or prove that all selectors are handled here. The old draft overstated this. We are keeping the original path as a starting point, but no longer deriving design conclusions from it.

JJC-212 records the identification of the first version in which Rebase revision subsets changed. The card later went through a risk review, so this page no longer treats "share revision selection results first" as the default approach. JJC-218 adds run records for Diffedit boundary revisions: observations should be made in an environment with no old cache or personal configuration, and paths that were or were not created should be recorded. The two cards provide different starting points for verification; they do not combine the two commands into one behavior.

## Keeping the old ideas here

There were initially two approaches.

The first was to obtain a set of revisions, then let the subsequent rebase or diffedit actions interpret the subset, boundary, and display content. The benefit is that selection results look reusable, and callers might only need to prepare one set of inputs. The problem is that once boundary handling is deferred to the action side, identical terminal displays do not mean the two entry points accepted the same scope.

The second was to keep each selection process separate and only use similar record formats for the two entry points. This approach is less convenient, but it does not erase input differences in advance. The old draft called it "sharing display and recording methods." That wording is still useful, but must no longer be read as sharing an implementation. Matching formats only make side-by-side reading easier; they are not enough to establish that candidate sets, actions, or path side effects are the same.

Neither approach has been selected. We are keeping both so that later results can answer a specific question: does the difference occur when locating revisions, or when interpreting actions? Without corresponding examples, command names cannot fill in that difference.

## Three separate columns for records

For Rebase examples, first record the revision submitted to the entry point, along with any destination, branch, source, and flags supplied with it. Do not assume the semantics of these terms here; only record whether they appear in the example and whether they change together with the results. Keep the raw terminal output in the second column. Record workspace changes separately in the third. That way, when output changes but paths do not, it will not be hastily classified as "the selection scope changed." Conversely, a path change alone cannot prove that the revision subset boundary was handled correctly.

Diffedit examples use the same three-column record, with environment conditions recorded separately. JJC-218 requires a check with no old cache and no personal configuration. Do not omit that condition and then extend the observation into a general conclusion. The path column must allow "not created." A path not being created is one possible observation result; it does not automatically mean failure, nor does it automatically mean the boundary revision was not recognized. Terminal text and path changes must be kept side by side; neither can be used to draw a conclusion on behalf of the other.

| Entry point | Inputs to record first | Results that must be saved side by side |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rebase revision subsets | revision, plus any destination, branch, source, and flags present in the example | Terminal output; workspace changes |
| Diffedit boundary revisions | Boundary-related inputs and the environment conditions of no old cache and no personal configuration | Terminal output; paths that were or were not created |

This table is only a recording convention, not a compatibility matrix. In particular, destination, branch, and source have not been established as shared fields. If they appear in examples for only one side, record that as it is rather than filling in values for the other side just to align the table.

## Merging we will not do in this round

Do not classify flags as "selector parameters" up front. The old draft proposed that direction, but no example shows whether flags change candidate revisions, terminal display, or subsequent actions. Classifying them early would remove the basis for comparison in later reviews. Likewise, destination, branch, and source cannot be treated as shared responsibility boundaries for the two entry points simply because they all appeared in the old search terms.

Do not fold Diffedit's path records into Rebase's success conditions either. Whether one entry point leaves a path is a post-action observation; whether the other displays a particular set of revisions is an interface-level observation. The two kinds of records can sit on the same page, but cannot vouch for each other. If comparable inputs and results do emerge on both sides later, we can discuss reusing selection logic. Until then, sharing is limited to the layout used to save examples.

## Conditions for deferral and withdrawal

If, with the revision input fixed, the subset result still cannot be separated from changes in destination or flags, do not use that example to support the first approach. If Diffedit only leaves terminal text in the specified environment and the path column consistently says not created, record only that observation; do not make path changes an interface commitment. In both cases, withdraw the push toward "revision selection results can be shared," rather than treating the absence of differences as evidence for merging.

Four points remain open: the hierarchy of destination, branch, and source; the scope of flags' effects; whether subset needs separate output; and what explanation Diffedit should retain when no path is created. These questions define the options under consideration on this page and cannot be answered by adjacent exception records. DOC-24 can serve as navigation to Abandon and backout boundaries, but does not supply Rebase or Diffedit results here.

This page still retains the old approaches because records for JJC-212 and JJC-218 will continue to be found from here. The statement that "the two entry points can share selection results" represents only the tentative idea at the time. If verifiable caller examples become available later, add them directly beside the corresponding approach and identify which record column they changed, rather than rewriting the old idea as an established fact.

# Remote and Path Compatibility Migration Procedure

This record originally just put three names together: Remote names and repository URLs, Push branch remote and revisions, and Unsquash and untrack paths. A later review found that although they all appeared in the completed work for JJ-2026.09, the things to check during migration are different. The first checks what the remote list left behind, the second checks whether the state is abnormal after combining the branch and revision, and the third checks what the path filter actually matched. Passing one action cannot replace checking the other two.

The relationship between the old entry points and the current review targets is shown here:

```text
Old investigation record
    -> internal/jj-completion-evolution / v_prev
    -> completers/git_completer/cmd/remote_setUrl.go

Current JJ-2026.09 review
    -> State before invocation
    -> Corresponding completion action
    -> Output, state, or path results
    -> Compare item by item with the old record
```

The file header in `completers/git_completer/cmd/remote_setUrl.go` retains `package cmd` and the import block. This file is an entry point for the earlier investigation, not grounds for automatically linking the three objects. During migration, start here to review the earlier observations, then switch to the actual output of the current completion action. If you can't find a corresponding result, leave it as "unconfirmed"; don't infer a relationship from similar filenames.

## Handle remote names and URL first

Checks for remote names and repository URLs start with the state before invocation. First record the remote name and repository URL visible at that point, then run the current completion action. When comparing, ask only two questions: can the candidate names still be selected, and does completion leave any additional visible changes? "The command didn't report an error" is not a substitute for the second check; no error only means the action finished, not that the names, URL, or subsequent display are exactly the same.

In the old records, this item was the earliest one raised on its own. The description of JJC-217 also starts by reproducing the pre-call state and confirming whether any additional visible changes remain after completion. The review record must therefore include, at a minimum, the name before the call, the selected URL, and the visible result after completion in the same entry. If there is no change, record "no additional visible changes"; if additional candidates, text, or status appear, record them as-is without attributing them to Push branch remote and revisions.

The migrated entry does not need to retain the old filename. What must be retained is the observation order: save the old-side input first, then inspect the current-side output. When the old record contains only a file path and partial navigation, it cannot be used to claim that the parsing, storage, or display of URL all takes place in that file.

## Pause on Push branch as a separate item

Push branch remote and revisions is not an ordinary naming difference in the old material. The phenomenon left by JJC-223 was an abnormal post-processing state, and the pending verification on the card asks the maintainer of the corresponding module to check the current-version behavior and identify where to continue the investigation. "Abnormal" must remain a description of the phenomenon; without new results, it must not be rewritten as a URL error, an incorrect revision selection, or a nonexistent remote.

2025-10-21 Added a counterexample. It changes how the review is done: don't take just one normal-branch sample through the entire flow and then explain the anomaly as incomplete input. First separate the counterexample from the normal path, and record the remote, branch, and revision combination and the post-action state for each. If they produce different results from the same entry point, the difference should remain at the sample level; if the current version still shows the anomaly, hand off the entry point for further investigation to the corresponding module maintainer.

The migration goal here isn't to hide the old anomaly. Preserve phenomena that can be reproduced through the old entry point. When the current entry point doesn't reproduce them, record only "the current sample did not reproduce it," not that the issue has been resolved. Conversely, don't delete new state changes that appear at the current entry point just because they weren't documented in the old record. This distinguishes old behavior, current behavior, and behavior that hasn't been matched yet.

## Verify Unsquash and untrack by path

Track entry-point updates for Unsquash and untrack paths in a separate record. During checks, use the repository's own path-checking command; don't add unconfirmed command names or parameters to this page. Keep two types of samples for every verification: a hit record showing that the given path actually entered the result, and a miss record showing that a similar but non-matching path was not included. Saving only "hit" records makes the post-migration boundary impossible to recheck; saving only "miss" records can't show that the entry point still works.

This work only began actual review on 2025-10-30 and was submitted for review on 11/4. What was added during that period was the check entry points and record format, not new conclusions about the behavior of all paths. If the hit and miss records use different path conditions, note the sample differences first; if neither record was retained, leave the gap in this item rather than filling it with results from Remote names.

The old and new sides can be compared in the following minimal sequence:

1. Retrieve the object names and original paths from old records; do not rewrite them into current terminology first.
2. At the current JJ-2026.09 entry point, prepare the pre-call state for the same type of call.
3. For Remote names and repository URLs, save the name, URL, and the visible result after completion.
4. For Push branch remote and revisions, also save the branch, remote, and revision combination, along with the state after the action; if an exception occurs, stop at the observed behavior.
5. For Unsquash and untrack paths, retain one matching case and one non-matching case.
6. Mark each item as "aligned," "not reproduced in the current sample," or "still unconfirmed"; do not combine the three into a single pass conclusion.

## Migrating and Restoring Old Paths

The old-side material for this migration is the `internal/jj-completion-evolution` snapshot of `v_prev`, with detailed navigation at `completers/git_completer/cmd/remote_setUrl.go`. It is suitable for reviewing how names, calls, and paths were found. The current side, in contrast, is based on the actual completed actions and results of JJ-2026.09. Both sides must retain the original object terms, especially remote, repository, branch, revision, unsquash, and untrack; do not leave only Chinese summaries.

If the current-side result is inconsistent with the old-side record, the recovery procedure is not to immediately modify the old material. First save the current output, identify whether the inconsistency occurred in the input, candidates, post-completion state, or path match, and then return to the old entry point to review the same object. Only after confirming that the entry-point selection after migration was incorrect should you revert to the old path and continue using the old record; if the current result merely differs from the old result, retain both results side by side and wait for confirmation from the module maintainer. Before confirmation, do not write the rollback up as a completed fix.

During recovery, pay particular attention to these three seemingly similar cases:

- The remote name can be listed, but the corresponding repository URL does not appear in the completion result;
- Candidates for Push branch remote and revisions appear, but the state remains abnormal after the action;
- The path text for Unsquash and untrack paths is similar, but only one of them actually matches.

They respectively concern names and URL, state changes, and path filtering, so they cannot share a single "migration failure" label. If only one of them can be confirmed, the other two remain unresolved as before.

## Retained entry points and responsibility boundaries

JJC-217 remains the reproduction entry point for Remote names; JJC-223 retains the anomalies and counterexamples for Push branch remote and revisions; JJC-225 retains the path inspection requirements for Unsquash and untrack paths. The three cards are only used to return to their respective local records; this page does not combine them into a new results table.

The interface side can sign off on its own completion results. When it crosses into the internals of an unconfirmed module, it should only record the issue and entry point. In particular, the Push branch anomaly cannot be signed off on the basis of the review result for remote URL. The conditions for an Unsquash match also cannot be inferred from the remote candidate rules. The items confirmed so far are the inspection order, sample separation, location of the old entry point, and recovery method; the specific implementation relationships remain subject to the file references in the current revision.

After the final review, this page adds a counterexample, a way to record the three objects separately, and the processing order for returning to the old entry point. Results that were not newly added remain explicitly blank: the current behavior of Push branch remote and revisions, the two actual-path records for Unsquash, and the as-yet-unverified reference relationship between the old file and the current implementation.

# Caller Dual-State Anomaly Postmortem

During integration testing with the caller, the same completers object showed different states at two entry points. This was not a discrepancy that disappeared after a single page refresh: reviewing the same set of real call samples showed that the old record and the later entry point were on different current revisions. The integrators therefore could not tell whether the object's state had changed or the content referenced by the entry point had been replaced.

The first recorded observation was that `repeatable positional` did not match the old record. At the time, that term only flagged a repeatedly observed difference in location; it did not say whether the discrepancy came from the command tree, the adapter layer, or the entry point. Later, someone tried subtracting one page output from the other directly. The resulting changes made it look as though caller behavior had switched; that comparison was not used further because the two outputs were not on the same revision.

The impact centered on judgments made during integration testing. The call samples originally used to confirm the adapter boundary still existed, but they could no longer be treated as continuous evidence for before-and-after trends. If later green results on the page masked the pre-recovery failure window, later investigators could mistakenly think the caller had never seen the old state. That risk is harder to handle than any single state value: the integration feedback would record a completed fix, when what actually remained were two observation points that could not be compared directly.

## Sequence of Events

At the first check, the record contained only the old entry point's results and a note on `repeatable positional`. Written alongside the incident notes was `@ fallback`; it was kept as a search marker used at the time, not treated as an explanation for the state discrepancy.

The current entry point then returned a different current revision. At that point, the focus shifted from retrying to preserving the original record: putting the two outputs side by side to avoid using the later entry point to rewrite the earlier failure window. For a time, the changed-path action was suspected as the direct source, but no evidence linking it to the state change was obtained. That suspicion was not treated as an established cause.

After that, the Cobra command tree was visible again on the recovery page. The recovery operation showed that the command tree could be returned to a usable state, but it did not prove that the object's displayed state had never changed, nor did it explain why the changed-path action changed. The second review still only verified the current entry point; no conclusions were added for branches that had not been reproduced.

Retries stopped once the command tree could be restored. This was not because the two entry points had been proven consistent, but because further refreshes would only produce more page results on different revisions. The original record, recovery results, and unconfirmed explanations were therefore kept separately.

## What Remained Open at the Time

This page retains a statement that later proved imprecise: the "current entry point" had been treated as the location of the state. The actual observations only established that it returned different current revisions at different checks; they did not support reconstructing the full sequence of changes to the completers object. The old wording was not deleted because it explains why the page discrepancy was misread as an adapter change at the time.

The change in the changed-path action remains unconfirmed. It may simply have coincided with the recovery, or it may have been related to the adapter boundary for the caller samples; the available records do not support choosing between the two. No follow-up comparison sufficient to cover the original failure window was run after the Cobra command tree was restored, so "recovery" was recorded only as a partial result.

Missing timestamp: ____

## Record Location

The original incident record remains at `docs/adj-completers/incidents/completers-client-integration-two-states-for-one-object.md`. When reviewing it, look at both the old record and the recovery page; do not use only the last successful output. This entry point preserves the actual samples, adapter boundaries, and integration feedback from integration testing with the caller; it does not fill in causal explanations for adjacent services.

If the same object shows two states again, first record the revision seen at each of the two entry points, then decide whether to compare the states. Without this step, new results will still get mixed in with the old window.

# Caller Exit Window Checklist

This window is reserved for the final checks for completers-client-integration. "Complete" in this checklist is not a release outcome, nor is it general acceptance of caller integration testing: it covers only the exit action, the last visible result, and the exit action for adj-completers; the relevant owner signs off separately on whether the release succeeded.

The entry point is still at `docs/adj-completers/release/completers-client-integration-window-exit-checklist.md`. Before starting, open the current record there, then create the working page for this window. If there is no current record, you may log the gap, but you must not reconstruct an exit result from the previous round's description.

## First Preserve the State When Entering the Window

The exit action will change the current state, so make the first record before taking action. Record at least:

- The completers-client-integration object being checked;
- Which status entry you see this time, and whether another status entry also remains in the checklist;
- Whether the current revision is in the record;
- The first visible result;
- Which exit entry point this attempt starts from, and whether it is actually accessible.

Here, "first visible result" means the result visible before the action occurs, not an all-green conclusion compiled after the fact. Do not clean up temporary states before recording them, and do not overwrite the first record with a later attempt. At the end of the window, compare the last recorded result before exit with the last recorded result after exit; list any intermediate exploratory operations separately if they changed the current state.

If two status entries appear for the same object, first copy both in the order they appeared, without merging them first. The checkpoint left by JJCA-002 concerns exactly such a dual-status object: at one point, the expiration action still pointed to the previous day's object. Similar status names and the same entry point are not sufficient to prove that they refer to the same object. If this cannot be confirmed, stop the exit check at object identification, record "Object relationship undetermined", and do not choose a seemingly newer status to proceed with closing the window.

## Window-Opening Actions

Follow the sequence below; any step may be a stopping point.

1. **Confirm the object.**
   Save both status entries side by side in the order they occurred. If only one is visible, explicitly state that only one is visible, and do not fill in a status for the other. If the relationship between the objects cannot be confirmed, do not perform the exit action.

2. **Confirm the record.**
   Check whether there is a corresponding window record for the current revision. The gap-handling approach in JJCA-013 is straightforward: if there is no record, explicitly state that no determination can be made. Do not assume that this revision has completed exit just because the entry point exists.

3. **Access the exit entry point.**
   Record whether the entry point opens, whether the action reaches the final step, and the first visible result. If the entry point only displays an intermediate state, retain that state as well; do not rewrite "can enter" as "has exited".

4. **Perform the exit action.**
   Perform it only for an object that has been confirmed. Immediately after the action, record the last visible result and retain the original pre-action record. This window does not require all caller statuses to be cleaned up, and its scope extends only to the exit action for adj-completers.

5. **Review before closing the window.**
   Review whether this window's object, action, and last visible result can be matched up. If there are still two status entries, or the action's target cannot be matched to the object, keep the window open and do not substitute "No new observations" for a result.

## When You Cannot Get Through the Entry Point

On one occasion, after switching accounts or workspaces, the operation stopped at the exit entry point. This must not be treated as "Exit completed but not documented". The record must preserve at least two things: whether the account or the workspace was changed, and whether the stop occurred before entering the entry point, within it, or after the exit action.

- Stops before entering the entry point: do not perform the exit action. Retain the existing object status and current revision, and mark the entry point as not reached.
- Entry point reachable, but no identifiable action result: do not perform cleanup, and do not treat the entry point being displayed as completion.
- Action has occurred, but the last visible result is missing: retain what is known from before and after the action, and do not sign off on the window; the release outcome still awaits the judgment of the relevant owner.
- Different results after switching back to the original account or workspace: record the two results separately. The later result must not overwrite the earlier one, because this difference itself is part of the window assessment.

Do not repeatedly switch accounts or workspaces just to make the checklist look tidy. The current material only shows that there was a stop at the exit entry point after switching one of the two, and you cannot infer from this that every account and every workspace will fail in the same way. If further attempts are needed, write the next attempt as a separate new record, and preserve the point where this attempt stopped.

## Expiration Actions and Handoff Records

The expiration action is not the only clue to the object being exited. Historical checks in JJCA-002 show that the expiration action may still apply to the previous day's object; it therefore serves only as a record that needs to be compared, and cannot by itself establish that the current object has exited.

JJCA-008 also revealed another mix-up: an expiration action was placed on the wrong card and was not from the same context as the "handoff record after the maintenance entry point is triggered". When this happens, proceed as follows:

- Leave that expiration action in its original record, without moving it under the object for the current window;
- Note in the window record that no correspondence has been established between it and the current context;
- Follow the maintenance entry point to find the actual person taking over, rather than treating "The project team will continue monitoring" as evidence that someone has taken over;
- Groups that have been taken offline must no longer be assigned to take over at new entry points.

The purpose of this step is not to reorganize all cards, but to prevent an action on the wrong card from incorrectly closing the current window. The other card can retain its own history; this page only needs to explain why it cannot be used as a criterion for this exit.

## Minimum Record Required for Sign-Off

Before closing the window, the working page should show the person taking over the following relationships:

| Item to check | What the window must retain | What cannot substitute for it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Object | One or two status entries and the order in which they occurred | Another record with a similar name |
| Exit action | An explicit status of performed, not performed, or not reached | Merely stating "Handled" |
| Last visible result | The actual final result remaining after the action | A success determination added after the fact |
| revision | A record exists, or an explicit statement that no record exists | Using a record from an old window in place of the current revision |
| Handoff | The actual person taking over as indicated by the maintenance entry point | "The project team will continue monitoring" |

"Not reached" in the table is a valid result. It indicates that this attempt did not get past the entry point; it should not be recast as a success status to be filled in later. "No record" in the table is also a valid result, but it prevents window sign-off until the relevant owner decides whether to conduct a follow-up check.

## Stopping and Recovery

Stop this exit verification if any of the following occurs: the object's dual statuses have not yet been confirmed, there is no record for the current revision, the exit entry point cannot be reached, the action result was not retained, or the expiration action is found to come from a different context.

After stopping, do not undo the original results already saved, and do not clean up cards that do not belong to the current object. The current checklist does not list the recovery action as a verified path: earlier records already note that the recovery action has not yet been tried in the shared environment. Therefore, when exit verification fails, the permitted response is to preserve the current state and stop; do not record an unverified recovery action as this window's rollback result.

If the relevant owner decides to start a separate recovery attempt, the new record should begin with the state before recovery and remain separate from this exit window. This preserves "where this attempt stopped" and prevents later recovery attempts from retroactively changing the assessment made at the time of the exit action.

## Include Only These Three Items in the Handoff

When handing off to the maintenance entry point, include the object status, the point reached in the exit action, and the last visible result. If there are two status entries, include both; if progress at the entry point stopped because of an account or workspace change, include the stopping point; if there is no record for the current revision, simply write "Unable to determine".

JJCA-013 are used to track follow-up checks for windows with no records, JJCA-002 are used to preserve checks of dual-status objects, and JJCA-008 are used to distinguish misfiled expiration actions from handoff records at the maintenance entry point. They provide navigation and do not replace the exit record on this page.

Finally, the relevant owner signs off separately on whether the release succeeded. This checklist extends only to the point where the exit window stops or the checks are completed.

# Proposed Approach for Caller Integration Testing

This approach ultimately did not make the adoption list. That assessment is retained because the comparison never had sufficient real-world caller evidence, viable recovery conditions, and a contrasting input all at the same time; it does not directly count any one blocked validation attempt as a failure of the candidate implementation. The original issue came from two actions within the same entry point: `external jj process` handles external processes, and `revision selector` handles revision selection. They have different exits when errors occur, which is why someone proposed moving the selector away from its position beside the original path. This starting point explains where the proposal came from, but does not imply that the old entry point must be replaced.

## How the approaches were laid out early on

Continuing with `external jj process` would let callers keep their usual way of entering and return to a familiar location during recovery. The cost is that selector exceptions would still sit alongside external process results, and reviewers would have to trace back through the entire completers-client-integration path to determine which action an exception belonged to. The early materials did not quantify this difficulty in locating failures; they only noted that the failure exits differed.

The other approach put `revision selector` into `Cobra command tree`, making it an independent action in the candidate tree. This might shorten the path from the output back to the failure location, or it might only change the presentation without actually changing the problem callers encounter. The candidate tree introduced a new way of entering, but no decision had been made on how to switch between the old and candidate entry points; there were also no clear steps establishing whether rollback would involve only restoring the old entry point. Which callers currently used `operation log` had not been verified either, and that scope cannot be inferred from the path name.

For that reason, v1 only said "leaning toward a split". At that point, there was no start date and no designated trial owner. Writing a limited-scope judgment up as an integration requirement would mislead readers into thinking the selector had already been moved out of the old entry point; this was also a limitation left intact when the original text was retained later.

## The v2 trial draft

The second version did not continue debating which entry point was more modern. Instead, it framed the comparison as a set of controls: one group would follow `external jj process`, while the other would use `Cobra command tree`. Both sides would use the same users, inputs, and observation window, changing only the entry point implementation. Each time, the original input, version, and first visible result would be preserved before checking whether callers could distinguish selection failures from external process failures. Aggregate results cannot replace the first firsthand observation, and tidier labels alone cannot count as a pass.

The proposal originally called for two weeks of observation. The success criteria were not reduced to a single green signal: locating failures needed to become faster, and misjudgments needed to stop recurring. Demonstrations without real callers, changes limited to display labels, and a single green result were all insufficient grounds for adoption. If locating failures did not improve, or if `Carapace action` could not be restored after leaving the candidate entry point, the candidate approach should be stopped and the old entry point restored. This recovery condition concerns the trial's fallback path; it does not mean that every behavior of the old entry point has been proven again.

The review also requested a contrasting input. The existing sample could at most show that it had produced some local result; it could not cover another category of input. Two labels, `candidate description` and `repeatable positional`, appeared in v2. They were useful for locating samples, but were not a substitute for a contrasting input and could not support a claim that the two approaches were already comparable. The contrasting input also needed to be rerun in an environment with the required permissions; otherwise, environmental restrictions would become mixed into the causes of failure.

## Reviewing the cards narrowed the comparison conditions

The action history for JJCA-003 recorded a reproduction on 2025-12-08, followed by a handling rationale stating that "the issue lies in another part of the implementation", with ownership adjusted accordingly on the card. This change split the early assumption into two questions: whether the selector was easier to identify, and whether the exception encountered by the caller actually came from the part of the implementation being examined. Improvement on the first question does not automatically answer the second. The card only supports retaining this distinction; it cannot be treated as a positive result for the candidate tree.

JJCA-009 underwent `rollback_checked` on 2025-12-11. The reason recorded later that day for changing the assignee was that the previous owner was not in the current cycle, so the current on-call person would handle it instead. What can be confirmed here is that the recovery action was checked, not that all callers had successfully rolled back from the candidate entry point. For the proposal, this meant the old entry point had to remain easy to find; it did not provide independent evidence for adopting or rejecting the candidate tree.

JJCA-014 moved into an in-progress state on 2026-01-05, with verification limited to the first `current revision` record after recovery, which later summaries were not to overwrite for the time being. A subsequent note on the card stated that "the due action's time is earlier than the original input", showing that the ordering of the input and recovery time had not yet been fully sorted out. By 2026-01-07, the item had become blocked because the account supplied by the caller lacked permissions in this environment. Without permissions, reliable caller samples cannot be obtained, and the candidate tree's behavior cannot be attributed to the command structure.

Taken together, the three cards showed that the original blanket description of "entry point failure" was not precise enough. The reproduction directed attention to another part of the implementation, the recovery check showed that the old entry point was still the actual fallback, the ordering issue with the first revision affected sample interpretation, and account permissions blocked subsequent calls. Collapsing these observations into "candidate tree failure" would mix implementation quality, the recovery path, and environment permissions into a single conclusion.

## What this version retains

For now, only a record of one proposal that was not adopted is retained: `Cobra command tree` was not written up as a plan to replace the original entry point soon, nor was splitting `revision selector` judged permanently infeasible. The original entry point, the candidate tree, and the difference in failure exits remain together in one place, making it easier to revisit why the trial was proposed at the time and preventing an unfinished experiment from being recast as a formal rule.

If a split is proposed again later, first obtain caller samples in an environment with the required permissions, and align the original input, version, recovery time, and first `current revision` after recovery. A contrasting input is also needed to observe whether the candidate tree actually separates selection failures from external process failures, rather than merely changing output names. If these conditions are not met, do not state again in the record that the two-week trial has begun, and do not switch entry points by default.

The scope of callers currently using `operation log` remains unconfirmed. JJCA-003, JJCA-009, and JJCA-014 captured firsthand evidence of reproduction, the recovery check, and the first record, respectively; they have not been combined into evidence that the approach passed. For subsequent discussions, start with three elements, `docs/adj-completers/proposals/rejected-completers-client-integration-approach.md`, the old entry point, and the selector, first fill in the missing real-world caller evidence, and then decide whether to reopen this proposal.

Each sample is recorded in three columns: the entrypoint originally used, the location to be replaced, and the caller actually using it. The third column matters more than the first two. A new entrypoint appearing in the directory, or an adapter file mentioning action, does not count as a completed migration; only when the caller confirms that it has switched to the alternative location do we mark the sample as migrated.

The callers in use had not yet been fully identified at the time, so we could not use `workspace registry` to infer a default batch of migration targets. 2. For that sample, add the alternative location for `changed-path action`, without merging in other side paths with similar names.
3. Once the actual caller confirms the entrypoint switch, change the sample from "pending migration" to "migrated." Leave the failure exit as-is with the sample so it is possible to distinguish whether the old entrypoint is still being called or the new action's adapter failed to handle it.
4. If the switch needs to be rolled back, first have that caller return to the old entrypoint, then remove this migrated marker from the index. Whether restoring only the old entrypoint was sufficient remained undecided at the time; do not treat one rollback as the outcome for the remaining callers.

Migration batches are tracked separately for each caller. Completing one sample does not automatically complete the other adapter locations in the same directory. # Run Monitoring Console Failure Runbook

This page starts with a actions-operations-observability run that has already encountered an anomaly. It covers two situations: after the window ends, the current entry point still shows the old value; or the actions · Operations Observability records on the two sides don't match. Get the existing run id, version, and trace before opening the page. Do not retry or clear records first.

## Enter the incident

The entry point is `docs/adj-actions/runbooks/actions-operations-observability-failed-run-on-call-page.md`. This file is the actions · Operations Observability knowledge base's latest-known export. The body and attachments are still maintained by adj-actions.

After opening it, first locate `revision selector` and confirm that the value it points to matches this run's version. If the selector is not visible, or its displayed version cannot be matched to the run id, stop at the entry point and record only the values shown on the page. Do not use an old value in the address bar as version evidence.

If you can access the run record, first save the few lines in `operation log` before the first anomaly, along with the anomalous node's trace. Preserve the original record. Do not delete, overwrite, or reorder it just to make the page green again. If you can see only the summary status, without the first anomalous node, stop as well; the summary status is not enough to decide on a recovery action.

## First branch

### The current entry point still has the old value

Record the current entry point exactly as it was when the window ended, then check whether it came from an old cache or an old task. Do not decide which of the two caused it at this stage. If the page shows both old and new records, compare their generation times and entry point values, and stop at the first difference. Do not treat the one that appeared later as a corrected version.

If there is only an old task and no new record for the same run id, stop further operations. On the on-call page, record only the old task identifier, version, trace, and the operation log from that time. Someone with visibility into that entry point's maintenance scope will need to confirm where the task came from.

### The records on the two sides don't match

Open each record. Compare the commands used to generate them and their timestamps first, then check the versions. If the commands match but the timestamps differ, keep both outputs and stop at the timestamp divergence. If the versions differ, treat the version difference as the first divergence. Do not use the success status in one record to overwrite the failure status in the other.

If one side has only `remote inventory` and the other has a run record, do not treat the inventory as a run result. Save its entry point value and the time you read it, then return to the side that can provide a run id to continue investigating. If neither side has the corresponding run id, stop here. You cannot infer from the page's color that the action has completed.

## After a failure appears

If the first failure is that `multipart candidate` did not appear, stop all subsequent recovery steps. Preserve the failed node's trace, version, and preceding output. Without this material, do not fill in "candidate generated." Recovery actions for this branch have not yet been tried in the shared environment. Do not change multiple conditions on the fly while on call.

If `multipart candidate` has appeared, but the later records end up at `@ fallback`, first save the raw fallback value and the immediately adjacent operation log. At this point, you can only confirm that the run reached this branch, not that it completed successfully. Before continuing, check that the version for the same run id is still consistent. If not, return to "The current entry point still has the old value" and stop.

If the record shows delegated completion, note it in the incident record only as the point the run has reached. It cannot replace the first failed node or erase the earlier old entry point value. Any recovery action must preserve the original records. This page has no recovery commands verified in the shared environment.

## Stop and hand off

Stop immediately if any of the following applies: the version cannot be confirmed at the entry point; the operation log does not include the first anomaly; the two records' generation times or commands cannot be compared; there is no new record for the same run id; or a new divergence appears after recovery. Include only what you actually observed in the handoff: run id, version, current entry point value, first failed node, trace, the two records' timestamps and commands (if available), and the step where you stopped.

If you need to roll back this attempt, preserve the original records of the old entry point and the return action. Do not create a separate "success" status on the on-call page. It must be possible to tell which version was used both before and after recovery. If you cannot confirm it, do not perform the return action. The next shift takes over from the maintenance page for the current entry point, first reading the stopping point left by this attempt, then deciding whether the conditions for a rerun are met.

The starting point for verification in this runbook remains the path above. If what you find does not match the steps in that path, stop at the failing step and record the specific object. Do not fill in missing steps with default values.

# Dependency Boundary Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

When the dependency boundary audit appears to stall at the entry point, first preserve what you saw the first time; do not rerun it immediately. Here, "stall" only means the current entry point does not provide a next destination that can be assessed; it does not mean the issue has already been traced to carapace-supply-boundary, nor does it mean the exit action failed.

First look in `docs/adj-carapace/runbooks/carapace-supply-boundary-blocked-escalation-contacts.md` for the config key from that time. If you can find it, look at it alongside the text left at the entry point; if you cannot, stop at the collection step and do not guess at downstream call relationships.

```text
Is there a record to preserve at the current entry point?
├─ No: capture a record, then check again
└─ Yes: can it be matched to a config key?
   ├─ Yes: continue investigating usage sites
   └─ No: stay on the entry-point side
```

The old practice was to clear the state and try again as soon as a usage contract appeared. This is no longer recommended as the first step: a normal result from a rerun cannot replace the original failing sample. When `repeatable positional` does not appear, do not infer the cause from directory names or displayed results either.

Only once the records extend beyond the current entry point should you distinguish between a problem inside carapace-supply-boundary, a problem with the exit action, and an issue the permissions side needs to take over. # Dependency Boundary Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

This page originally only covered cases where the entry point stopped producing output. During a handoff, the detail most easily lost is not who ultimately owns the issue, but where the first difference appeared: some people start looking based on directory names, some rerun first, and others see one green result and treat the case as recovered. The last two approaches leave later comparisons without a reference.

First, keep the raw record from the entry point separate. At a minimum, it must show which node was reached at the time, which side's environment was used, and the first visible result. There is no requirement to fill in the entire call chain here; if you determine that you cannot proceed, the record itself is the endpoint for this node.

## Check the tree before deciding who takes over

```text
Entry point stops at the dependency boundary audit
│
├─ No raw record
│  └─ Collect it; do not discuss root cause or take exit actions
│
├─ Raw record exists, but no matching config key can be found
│  └─ Return to the entry-point side to verify the record; stop here
│
└─ Record exists and config key can be found
   │
   ├─ Matches the most recent known-good sample from the Cobra command tree
   │  ├─ Entry point or environment differs: keep the investigation on the entry-point/environment side
   │  └─ No first difference yet: do not substitute average behavior for a comparison
   │
   └─ Does not match the Cobra command tree
      ├─ First difference is still within carapace-supply-boundary: continue within the project
      └─ Difference crosses an explicit interface: hand off to the other side of the interface
```

"Most recent known-good sample" does not mean a default baseline set here. It is used only to find the first point where the paths diverge. If the two samples use different environments, write down the environment differences first, then decide whether the comparison is worthwhile. Combining all results into a single summary value usually obscures whether the entry point changed, the command tree changed, or the record came from somewhere else.

The old draft treated `Cobra command tree` as the overall entry point, which was too broad. On this page, it is only a comparison point: when the raw record already points to the command tree, compare it step by step with the known-good sample; when the raw record stops at an earlier entry point, do not use the command tree to fill in an intermediate node that was never observed.

## While the record is still within the project

If the config key matches and the first difference is still within carapace-supply-boundary's own scope, continue to retain the original input, version, and first result. At this point, you can check whether the Carapace action has been reached, but do not assume it is the root cause just because it appears in the name.

A Carapace action becomes a handoff point under only one condition: the user-visible contract across the interface needs to change. Differences limited to project-internal resources, permissions, or indexes still stay within the project. The old version handed things off as soon as an action was seen; it later turned out that this also carried along entry-point issues that had not yet been localized. Now, first ask whether the first difference has crossed an interface.

Change only one condition per troubleshooting round. That condition can be the entry point, environment, or comparison sample, but do not change all three at once and then explain the result. If a rerun goes green, keep it as a lead for follow-up, with the initial record alongside it; do not let the green result overwrite the original stall.

## Exit-action branch

Do not take exit actions at the start. First confirm that the record has actually reached the point where the old relationship needs to be withdrawn; if you cannot yet tell whether the old relationship is involved, taking an exit action only introduces another change.

When investigating withdrawal of the old relationship, you can start with the replay items in JJCC-011. This entry point focuses on whether the old edge remains after withdrawal; it does not replace the record comparison above. If the old edge remains, first retain the records from before and after replay. If there are not enough records to establish whether it existed before, stop at collection rather than writing "not seen" as "already gone."

## What to leave before handing off

When handing off to the other side, include just three things: the initial raw record, the first difference reached in the comparison, and the reason the investigation did not proceed further. Do not write speculation as a confirmed interface change. If you can clearly say "the difference is still within this project," keep handling it within the project; only when you can clearly say "the difference has crossed the interface" should you hand those three items to the other side of the interface.

The task for comparing the current revision with an adjacent one is in JJCC-004. It calls for selecting just one adjacent revision with a working path and comparing the first point where the paths diverge. This is appropriate when a raw record already exists; without one, collecting the record first is more useful than selecting more revisions.

The toolchain was pinned at one point, so path differences in old records should not automatically be applied to a new toolchain. That old hint is retained here so that whoever takes over does not assume all differences come from the current entry point; it is not a conclusion about the existing environment.

The handoff materials are still in `docs/adj-carapace/runbooks/carapace-supply-boundary-blocked-escalation-contacts.md`. DOC-41 documents a case that is still open; if you need to follow up on the raw record, you can start with that page for context.
